DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On May 7, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Anna Hamburg-Gal issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) recommending the dismissal of the majority interest
petition filed by Petitioner Chicago Fire Fighters Union, Local 2, IAFF (“Union”), which seeks to
include employees in the titles Deputy District Chief (“DDC”) and Assistant Deputy Chief
Paramedic1 to its historical unit of uniformed members of Respondent City of Chicago, Fire
Department (“Employer”). The ALJ recommended dismissal of the Petition, finding that the DDCs
are above the highest-ranking company officer and thus, are supervisory employees within the
meaning of Section 3(r) of the Act. The ALJ further found that, should the Board determine that the
DDCs are not above the highest-ranking company officer, none of the DDCs satisfied the four-part
supervisory test. She also determined that certain of the DDCs were not managerial employees and
that certain others fell within the managerial and confidential employee exclusions.
Petitioner filed exceptions challenging the ALJ’s determinations and conclusions resulting in
the recommendation to dismiss the Petition.2 Specifically, Petitioner takes exception to the ALJ’s
1 On February 6, 2024, Petitioner withdrew its petition with respect to the Assistant Deputy Chief Paramedic title.
2 On June 12, 2025, we granted Petitioner leave to file its exceptions instanter.
1

determinations on the company office issue, her findings that the DDCs exercise supervisory
authority with independent judgment, and determination that DDC Mark Kiely is a managerial
employee excluded from the Act’s coverage. The City filed responses to Petitioner’s exceptions and
cross-exceptions to the ALJ’s alternative findings that the DDCs are not supervisors under the four-
part supervisory test and her determinations regarding the managerial employee exclusion, to which
Petitioner filed cross-responses.3 Due to the significance and novelty of the company officer issue
and upon Petitioner’s request, the matter was scheduled for oral argument, which was held at the
Board’s October 23, 2025 meeting.
Upon consideration of the record, the RDO, the exceptions, responses thereto, supporting
briefs, and the parties’ oral arguments, we find as follows:
3 On June 23, 2025, Respondent timely filed responses to Petitioner’s exceptions and also filed cross-exceptions.
Petitioner then filed a document titled “Petitioner’s Cross-Responses and Reply to Employer’s Response to Union’s
Exceptions and Cross-Exceptions to Administrative Law Judge’s Recommended Decision and Order” (“Petitioner’s
Cross-Responses”). This last submission triggered the following procedural motions, responses, and replies, as titled by
the respective party: (1) Respondent’s Motion to Strike Portions of Petitioner’s Cross-Response and Reply
(“Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply”); (2) Petitioner’s Response to Employer’s Motion to Strike Portions of
Petitioner’s Cross-Response and Reply and Cross-Motion to Strike (“Petitioner’s Response to Motion to Strike 1”); (3)
Respondent’s Response to Petitioner’s Request for Variance, in the Alternative (“Response to Request for Variance”);
(4) Petitioner’s Reply to Respondent’s Response to Request for Variance in the Alternative (“Reply to Response to
Request for Variance”); and (5) Respondent’s email moving to strike Petitioner’s Reply to Respondent’s Response to
Request for Variance in the Alternative (“Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply 2”).
On August 14, 2025, we granted, in part, Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply 1, and denied Petitioner’s request
for a variance. Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply 1 was granted to the extent that Section II.A of Petitioner’s Cross
Responses was stricken as a reply to Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s exceptions. Section II.A, pages 2-9, of
Petitioner’s Cross-Responses is tantamount to a reply to Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s exceptions. That section
specifically references arguments contained in Respondent’s responses to Petitioner’s exceptions and cannot be read to
serve any other purpose than as a reply to Respondent’s responses to Petitioner’s exceptions to the RDO. The first
paragraph of Section II.A. begins by asserting that the “City erroneously argues that that the ALJ correctly found that the
Deputy District Chiefs (“DDC”) are supervisors within the meaning of the Act because they hold a rank above that of
the highest company officer” citing a page from Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s exceptions. (Petitioner’s Cross-
Response, p. 2). The remainder of that section is replete with argument related to Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s
exceptions to the ALJ’s determinations regarding the company officer issue. The Board’s rules do not provide for replies
to responses to exceptions or appeals. See 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135. As Respondent observes, recently, and under
similar circumstances, the Board’s State Panel struck a party’s reply to the opposing party’s response to exceptions that
was filed without leave to do so. See., e.g., Univ. Park Prof’l Fire Fighters Ass’n, 41 PERI ¶ 146 (IL LRB-SP 2025)
(striking a reply to response to exceptions filed without leave or a variance from the Board’s rules). Here, Petitioner
neither moved for leave to file a reply nor requested a variance from the Board’s rules before filing the reply.
2

Company Officer Issue
The key issue in this case is whether the DDCs qualify as company officers. The ALJ
determined that, in the event we determine that they are the highest rank of company officers, the
DDCs are not supervisors under the four-part supervisory test found in the first paragraph of Section
3(r)(1) of the Act. Resolving the company officer issue involves interpretation of language in the
second paragraph of Section 3(r)(1), amended by Public Act 102–686 (P.A. 102-686, eff. June 1,
2022) (“2022 Amendment”). The second paragraph of Section 3(r)(1) states as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding paragraph, in
determining supervisory status in fire fighter employment, no fire fighter
shall be excluded as a supervisor who has established representation rights
under Section 9 of this Act. Further, in new fire fighter units, employees
shall consist of fire fighters of the highest rank of company officer and
below. A company officer may be responsible for multiple companies
or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire shift. There may
be more than one company officer per shift. If a company officer
otherwise qualifies as a supervisor under the preceding paragraph,
however, he or she shall not be included in the fire fighter unit. If there is
no rank between that of chief and the highest company officer, the employer
may designate a position on each shift as a Shift Commander, and the
persons occupying those positions shall be supervisors. All other ranks
above that of the highest company officer shall be supervisors.”
5 ILCS 315/3(r)(1). (Relevant changes noted by strikethrough text and bolded underline).
The ALJ found that the plain meaning and legislative history of the 2022 Amendment did not
change or expand the definition of “company officer” established by Board and court precedents,
which hold that “company officer” refers to an employee who oversees a company, i.e., personnel
assigned to a vehicle, equipment, or ambulance. See City of Freeport v. Ill. State Labor Relations
Bd., 135 Ill.2d 499, 522 (1990); Vill. of Elk Grove Vill. v. Ill. State Labor Relations Bd., 245 Ill.
App. 3d 109, 211 (2d Dist. 1993); City of Evanston, 5 PERI ¶ 2023, fn. 6 (IL SLRB 1989). The ALJ
noted that the legislative discussion of the 2022 Amendment implicitly affirmed the Board’s decision
in Village of Palatine, 25 PERI ¶ 114 (IL LRB-SP 2009), where the Board included the Village of
3

Palatine’s captains in the existing bargaining unit as company officers because they functioned as
company officers “no differently” than the lieutenants who had immediate responsibility for
personnel assigned to one or more companies. Id. She then concluded that the DDCs are above the
highest rank of company officer.
Petitioner’s Exceptions and Employer’s Response
Petitioner takes exception to the ALJ’s determinations on the company office issue,
contending that the ALJ erred in concluding that the DDCs are above the highest rank of company
officer. Petitioner focuses on the following language of the 2022 Amendment: “A company officer
may be responsible for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an
entire shift. There may be more than one company officer per shift.” It contends that this
language expands the definition of company officers to include those employees who “may be
responsible” for more than one company or apparatus on a shift, one station, or for an entire shift. In
addition to Village of Palatine, 25 PERI ¶ 114 ( ILRB-SP 2009), the Union contends that the 2022
Amendment was passed in response to City of Rolling Meadows, 34 PERI ¶ 81 (ILRB-SP G.C. Order,
Oct. 14, 2017), in which a Board ALJ excluded Battalion Chiefs because they held a rank above that
of the lieutenants who served as company officers. In support of its claim that the intent of the 2022
Amendment was to include those officers in ranks that were responsible for more than one crew or
apparatus, Petitioner points to the ALJ’s finding there that the lieutenants’ connection to a single
apparatus or crew is determinative of company officer status. In the instant case, Petitioner asserts
that the DDCs who are responsible for multiple companies, apparatus on a shift, stations, and the
entire shift in their respective districts, satisfy this expanded definition of company officer. The
Petitioner further asserts that the DDCs share these responsibilities with their subordinate Battalion
Chiefs.
4

The Employer responds that the ALJ correctly analyzed the language of the 2022 Amendment
and its legislative history in finding that the DDCs are above the highest-ranking company officer. It
asserts that the evidence, including testimony from the DDCs, failed to demonstrate that the DDCs
serve as company officers, so the DDCs cannot be the highest-ranking company officers. The
Employer contends that the 2022 Amendment did not remove or change the meaning of company
officer as defined in previous Board rulings and caselaw. The 2022 Amendment merely clarified that
that “company officers” may include individuals like the captains in Village of Palatine and did not
provide a “new definition” of company officer. Furthermore, the Employer points out that the
Department does not consider the DDCs to be company officers and the DDCs do not consider
themselves to be company officers. Finally, the Employer contends that Petitioner failed to take
exception to the ALJ’s findings on the highest rank immediately responsible for crew on the fire side
and on the EMS side of the department, and thus, has waived its right to do so.4
We find merit to Petitioner’s exceptions to the ALJ’s findings and determinations on the
company officer issue. In finding that the DDCs are above the highest ranking company officer, the
ALJ took the approach that the amendatory language “may be responsible for multiple companies or
apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire shift” was intended to “convey that these were
potential functions of a company officer rather than proof of company officer status,” and that the
plain language “preserved the existing definitions of “companies” and “company officer” established
by the courts and the Board rather than rejecting the common understanding of that term used in
previous decisions.
4 We find that Petitioner did not waive its right to take exception to the ALJ’s findings on the highest rank immediately
responsible for crew on the fire side and on the EMS side of the department. We find that Petitioner’s exception to the
ALJ’s finding that the DDCs occupy a rank above that of the highest rank of company officer effectively disputes the
ALJ’s findings in question.
5

We find, however, that the amendatory language used by the legislature expresses the intent
to broaden the definition of “company officer” to include those employees, in this case the DDCs,
who are “responsible for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire
shift” without necessarily finding that the amendment rejects the common understanding of company
officer to mean the employee responsible for a single company or crew.
The ALJ found support for her interpretation of the express language in the legislative history
of the 2022 Amendment, citing a portion of Representative Lawrence Walsh’s opening statement in
support of House Bill 220, in which he stated:
By adding this language that the company officer may be responsible
for the things mentioned above, it basically is changing the definition
of what a company officer is and clarifying that and going along with
the ruling from the Illinois Labor Relations Board
Illinois House Transcript, 2021 Reg. Sess. No. 19, at pp. 53-54. The ALJ noted that the legislative
discussion of the 2022 Amendment supports the interpretation of the language as clarifying rather
than rejecting the common understanding of the term “company officer.” Although Rep. Walsh did
not identify the “ruling from the Illinois Labor Relations Board” to which he was referring, the ALJ
found an implicit reference to the Board’s decision in Village of Palatine. The ALJ observed that
implicit in the Board’s determination that the Village of Palatine’s captains were company officers,
was the captains’ “immediate responsibility of the personnel of one or more crews (engines and
ambulances) either by virtue of being ‘in charge of’ a station that was comprised of those crews or
by being ‘in charge of’ the crew on a particular piece of equipment at an incident.” (RDO, p. 42).
We disagree with the ALJ’s interpretation of the amendatory language. The 2022 Amendment
does not use the word “immediate” or “immediately” to qualify how a company officer “may be
responsible for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire shift, and
the word “immediate” or “immediately” does not appear in the legislative discussions in describing
6

such responsibilities. Had the legislature intended to limit the company officer designation to those
employees who had “immediate” responsibility for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift,
multiple stations, or an entire shift, it could have used “immediately” to describe “may be responsible
for” in amending Section 3(r)(1). But the legislature did not do so, and we decline to read into the
plain language of the amendment terms or limitations not expressed by the legislature in amending
the statute. Petersen v. Wallach, 198 Ill. 2d 439, 446 (2002).
Our interpretation of the express language is consistent with the purposes and policies of the
Act, construing the amended supervisory exclusion in Section 3(r)(1) to extend collective bargaining
rights broadly. See City of Decatur v. Am. Fed’n of State, Cnty., & Mun. Emps., Local 268, 122 Ill.
2d 353 (1988). It also finds support in the legislative discussions. Representative Walsh notes that
HB 220 was initiated by the IAFF “in response” to a decision from the Board. It is likely that the
decision to which he was referring is the non-precedential final order in City of Rolling Meadows,
34 PERI ¶ 81, issued in 2017 and closer in time to the 2022 Amendment, which was not favorable to
unions seeking to include employees in firefighter units because company officer status was limited
to responsibility for just one company or crew, rather than the Board’s decision in Village of Palatine,
issued in 2009, that found in favor of the petitioning union where the number of companies was not
expressly determinative. As noted above, in City of Rolling Meadows, the ALJ found the lieutenants’
connection to a single apparatus or crew determinative of company officer status in excluding
Battalion Chiefs who the ALJ observed “are never directly tied to just one crew or apparatus.” City
of Rolling Meadows, 34 PERI 81. In Village of Palatine, however, the Board found the captains in
that case to be company officers because they were responsible for one station or company nearly as
often as the lieutenants who were considered company officers. Vill. of Palatine, 25 PERI ¶ 114.
7

Accordingly, we reject the ALJ’s findings and recommendations on the company officer issue
and find that the DDCs are company officers under the express language of Section 3(r)(1) of the
Act.
Supervisory and Managerial Exclusions
The ALJ noted that should we find that the DDCs are not above the highest rank of company
officer, she would find that none of the DDCs satisfy the four-part supervisory test. The ALJ observed
that although the principal work of the DDCs is obviously and visibly different from that of their
subordinates and they exercise certain supervisory authority with independent judgment when
performing particular job duties, none of the DDCs spend a preponderance of their time exercising
supervisory authority under either a quantitative or qualitative test.
Next the ALJ determined that the Special Operations DDCs Jason Lach, Douglas Schick, and
Davide Doggett, Training Division DDC Richard Stack, and Fire Prevention DDC Evan Person are
not managerial employees within the meaning of the Act. She observed that none of these petitioned-
for employees predominantly engaged in executive and managerial functions or are responsible for
effectuating management policies and practices. The ALJ did, however, conclude that the DDC for
the Mobile Reporting Unit (“MRU”), Mark Kiely, should be excluded as a managerial employee
under Section 3(j) of the Act.
We reject as meritless, Petitioner’s exceptions to the ALJ’s findings regarding the 4-part
supervisory test and managerial employee test as well as the Employer’s cross-exceptions and accept
the ALJ’s alternative findings and recommendations that the DDCs are not supervisors under the 4-
part supervisory test. In addition, we accept the ALJs’ recommendations regarding managerial status
for the employees and positions listed on page 85 of the RDO.
8

For the above reasons, we reject the ALJ’s recommendations regarding the company officer
issue and find that the DDCs are company officers within the meaning of Section 3(r)(1) of the Act.
In addition, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations that the DDCs are not supervisors under the 4-
part supervisory test of Section 3(r) of the Act and that certain DDCs are not managerial employees
under Section 3(j) of the Act. Finally, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations that DDC Mark Kiely
is a managerial employee excluded from collective bargaining under Section 3(j) of the Act and that
the position of DDC – Manpower Division is excluded from bargaining as confidential under Section
3(c) of the Act.
We direct the Executive Director to certify Petitioner as the exclusive representative of the
bargaining unit as described in the Petition and consistent with the findings set forth in this Decision
and Order.

Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) recommending dismissal of the unit clarification
petition filed by Petitioner State of Illinois, Department of Central Management Services, seeking to
exclude a newly created and vacant Administrative Assistant II position within the Department of
Innovation and Technology from an existing bargaining unit represented by the American Federation
of State, County, and Municipal Employees, Council 31 (“Union”). Petitioner filed exceptions to the
RDO, and the parties presented oral arguments on October 23, 2025.

Curiae (“Amicus Brief”) along with a copy of the brief in support of the Union’s position that it seeks

be beneficial to our consideration and resolution of the issues presented. We further find that

For the above reasons, we grant the Motion for Leave to File a Brief Amicus Curiae and

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On April 3, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed an unfair labor practice
charge filed by Charging Party Mary White on February 3, 2025. Charging Party is employed by
the Will County Sheriff’s Department (“Employer”), as a Deputy Correctional Officer and is a
member of a bargaining unit represented by the Respondent, the American Federation of State,
County, and Municipal Employees, Council 31 (“AFSCME” or “Union”). Charging Party alleges
that AFSCME engaged in unfair labor practices within the meaning of Section 10(b) of the Act by
failing to keep her apprised of the status of her grievance over her June 2022 discharge.
The Executive Director dismissed the charge on grounds that Charging Party failed to
comply with requests for information made by the Board agent investigating the charge. Noting
the intentional misconduct standard in duty of fair representation cases and a union’s discretion
in contract interpretation and grievance handling under Section 6(d) of the Act, the Executive
Director also determined that the evidence initially submitted with the charge failed to indicate
that AFSCME engaged in any intentional misconduct.
1

Charging Party timely appealed. AFSCME did not file a response. On appeal, Charging
Party acknowledges receipt of the information requests and regrets that she did not provide the
requested information. She asserts, however, that she can provide further evidence such as emails,
medical records, and a witness willing to testify to AFSCME’s misconduct.
Upon review of the record, the dismissal order, and the appeal, we affirm the dismissal of
the charge for Charging Party’s appeal is meritless. Although she acknowledges receipt of the
Board agent’s requests for information in support of the charge, Charging Party fails to explain
her failure to provide the requested information. Section 1220.40(a)(1) of the Board’s rules require
charging parties to submit all relevant evidence supporting a charge. 80 Ill. Adm. Code §
1220.40(a)(1). As the Executive Director correctly noted, the Board has interpreted this rule to
provide a basis for dismissal of an unfair labor practice charge when a charging party has not
complied with a request for information. See, e.g., State of Ill., Dep’t of Cent. Mgmt. Servs. (Dep’t
of Rehab. Servs.), 12 PERI ¶ 2005 (IL SLRB 1995), aff’d sub nom Kirk et al. v. State of Ill. Cent.
Mgmt. Servs. (Rehab. Servs.), 13 PERI ¶ 4008 (1996) (unpublished order under Supreme Court
Rule 23) (sustaining dismissal for failure to comply with request for information in support of an
unfair labor practice charge.). Moreover, nothing in Charging Party’s appeal serves to undermine
the Executive Director’s determination on the merits of the allegations based on the evidence
submitted with the charge. Accordingly, we find that the Executive Director correctly dismissed
the charge.

For the above reasons, we affirm the dismissal for the reasons stated by the Executive

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On April 16, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Donald Anderson issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) concluding that Respondent Chicago Transit Authority
(“CTA” or “Employer”) did not engage in unfair labor practices in violation of Section 10(a) of the
Illinois Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., as alleged by Charging Party Erek
Slater. On June 20, 2025, Charging Party filed two documents, one titled “Charging Party’s
Exceptions to Administrative Law Judge’s Recommended Decision and Order” (“Exceptions”), and
the other titled “Charging Party’s Brief in Support of Exceptions to Administrative Law Judge’s
Recommended Decision and Order” (“Supporting Brief”), challenging the ALJ’s recommendations.
Respondent then filed a Motion to Strike Charging Party’s Exceptions and Brief in Support of
Exceptions (“Motion to Strike”), contending that Charging Party’s filings do not comport with the
requirements set by Section 1200.140(b) of the Board’s Rules and Regulations (“Board’s Rules”).
Charging Party filed a response to Respondent’s Motion to Strike and filed a Motion for Section
1200.160 Variance of the Rules and Leave to Re-File Combined Exceptions and Brief in Support of
Exceptions with Request for Oral Argument on Exceptions (“Motion for Variance and Leave”).
Respondent filed a timely response to Charging Party’s Motion for Variance and Leave.
1

Respondent’s Motion to Strike
Respondent moves to strike Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting Brief, contending
that such filings total 89 pages, exceeding the 50-page limit set forth in Section 1200.40(b) of the
Board’s Rules. The Respondent further asserts that Charging Party’s Exceptions, totaling 61 pages,
is also a “brief” because it contains argument in support of each exception included in that document.
Respondent contends that Charging Party has thus filed two briefs, without leave to do so, which is
not allowed under the Board’s Rules. Respondent also contends that Charging Party filed the 61-
page Exceptions, which exceeds the 50-page limit set forth in Section 1200.140(b) without leave to
do so. In support, Respondent points to other instances where Charging Party’s filings have skirted
the rules, such as the filings related to Charging Party’s motion to amend the complaint and the filing
of Charging Party’s post-hearing brief. Respondent urges the Board to strike both documents due to
the difficulty in deciding which pages of the documents to strike.
In his response, Charging Party asserts that Section 1200.135(b) and Section 1200.140
contemplate that exceptions are separate documents from briefs in support of exceptions because
Section 1200.140(a)(3) defines “Briefs” in terms of “briefs in support of exceptions” and omits
“exceptions” in that definition. (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 5). Charging Party notes that Section
1200.140(a)(3) defines “briefs in support of exceptions” as “inclusive of any separate exceptions [ .
. .] filed with the brief” and contends that a reasonable reading of that definition is that “Section
1200.143(a)(3) contemplates a ‘brief’ with exceptions separate and additional to the exceptions
already filed in a party’s ‘exceptions’ document and therefore only ‘filed with the brief’ not with the
‘exceptions’.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16). Charging Party reasons that “there would be no
need to identify a ‘brief in support of exceptions’ absent ‘exceptions’ that the brief was directed
2

toward supporting.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16). Charging Party further states that “the
contemplation of ‘separate exceptions’ that are ‘filed with the brief’ is reasonable in that some
exceptions may not need extensive argument and therefore would not require a party to duplicate an
‘exception’ in an ‘exception’ document and in a brief.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16). As such,
Charging Party argues that the 50-page limit set forth in Section 1200.140(b) applies only to
supporting briefs and does not include a page limit for exceptions when they are filed as a separate
document. Charging Party further asserts that his counsel conducted extensive research and found
no cases on this issue. Charging Party also states that his counsel consulted other attorneys who have
filed separate exceptions and contends that they have filed exceptions in addition to a supporting
brief which, when combined, totaled more than 50 pages.
Charging Party’s Motion for Variance and Leave to Re-File
Charging Party seeks a variance from the Board’s Rules that govern filing deadlines for
exceptions and page limits for briefs and requests leave to re-file its exceptions and brief as a single
document not exceeding 60 pages. Charging Party contends all three criteria for granting variances
are satisfied: (1) the rules are not statutorily mandated; (2) Respondent would not be prejudiced by
granting a variance as Respondent has already previewed Charging Party’s arguments and can more
readily respond to them; and (3) it would unreasonable and duly burdensome for the Board to strictly
adhere to these rules where the consequences of striking his exceptions would constitute a waiver of
his challenges to the RDO.
Respondent opposes Charging Party’s motion. Respondent contends that Charging Party
“confuses quantity with complexity” and claims that the reason the record contains multiple volumes
of testimony and exhibits can be attributed to Charging Party’s litigation strategy to “muddy
the record.” Respondent asserts that allowing Charging Party to re-file as a single, combined
exceptions and supporting brief document totaling 50 pages would prejudice Respondent because it
3

would then need to seek leave to respond to Charing Party’s over-sized exceptions and supporting
brief with its own over-sized response.
Discussion
Both motions revolve around Sections 1200.135(b) and 1200.140 of the Board’s Rules.
Section 1200.135(b) outlines the process and requirements for the Board’s review of an ALJ’s RDO
and provides in relevant part:
b) Administrative Law Judge's Recommended Decision and Order
1) Proceedings
* * * *
B) In unfair labor practice proceedings, parties may file
exceptions to the Administrative Law Judge’s
recommended decision and order, and briefs in support of
those exceptions, no later than 30 days after service of the
recommended decision and order. . . .
C) In either type of proceeding, exceptions, responses,
cross-exceptions, cross-responses and briefs, shall be filed
with the Board’s General Counsel in the Board's Chicago
office. A party not filing timely exceptions waives its right
to object to the Administrative Law Judge’s recommended
decision and order.
* * * *
2) Exceptions and/or cross-exceptions shall specifically set
forth the questions of procedure, fact, law or policy to
which exception is taken, shall identify that part of the
Administrative Law Judge's recommended decision and
order to which objection is made, and shall state the
grounds for the exceptions and shall include the citation of
authorities and citations to the record unless set forth in a
supporting brief. Any exception to a ruling, finding,
conclusion or recommendation that is not specifically
urged shall be deemed to have been waived. Any exception
that fails to comply with the foregoing requirements may
be disregarded.
3) Any brief in support of exceptions shall be confined to the
subjects raised in the exceptions and shall contain:
A) a clear and concise statement of the case containing all
that is material to the consideration of the questions
4

presented;
B) a specification of the questions involved and the issues
to be argued; and
C) an argument, presenting clearly the points of fact and
law relied upon in support of the position taken on each
question.
* * * *
80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2) and (b)(3) (emphasis added). Section 1200.135(c) provides that
“Parties desiring oral argument before the Board shall request oral argument and state the reasons for
the requests in their appeals, exceptions and responses. . . .” 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(c)
(emphasis added).
Section 1200.140(a) states in relevant part:
a) For purposes of this Section, “briefs” shall be deemed to
include:
* * * *
3) briefs in support of exceptions and cross-exceptions to an
Administrative Law Judge's recommended decision and order
and responses to that decision and order, inclusive of any
separate exceptions, cross-exceptions or response document
filed with the brief;
* * * *
b) All briefs, including supporting materials, shall be no more than
a total of 50 double-spaced pages with margins of at least ½
inch, including attachments. All of the pages in excess of the 50
page limit will be rejected, unless leave is granted. In the
extraordinary circumstance that a case involves extremely
complex issues, issues of first impression, or a lengthy factual
record, a party may seek leave to file a brief in excess of 50
pages by filing a motion requesting leave. Motions seeking
leave must be filed before the deadline for filing the brief at
issue and should be directed to the Administrative Law Judge
with whom the brief is pending or the General Counsel if the
brief is on a matter before the Board.
80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.140(a) and (b) (emphasis added).
5

For the reasons discussed below, we grant Respondent’s Motion to Strike but also grant
Charging Party’s motion for a variance to re-file its Exceptions and Supporting brief as a single
document comprising 60 pages within five business days of service of the Board’s order.
Although the Board’s Rules recognize that exceptions may be filed as a separate document
and do not set a page limit specifically on “exceptions” per se, Section 1200.140(b) clearly defines
“Briefs” to include “briefs in support of exceptions . . . , inclusive of any separate exceptions, cross-
exceptions or response document filed with the brief.” 80 Ill. Adm. Code §1200.140(a)(3) (emphasis
added). And because Section 1200.140(b) limits all briefs, including supporting material to 50 pages,
absent leave to file a brief in excess of that page limit, Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting
Brief do not comport with Section 1200.140(b) of the Board’s Rules.1
We are unpersuaded that Charging Party’s interpretation of Section 1200.140(a)(3) is a
reasonable interpretation of the that rule. Charging Party states that “Section 1200.143(a)(3)
contemplates a ‘brief’ with exceptions separate and additional to the exceptions already filed in a
party’s ‘exceptions’ document and therefore only ‘filed with the brief’ not with the ‘exceptions’,”
and reasons that “there would be no need to identify a ‘brief in support of exceptions’ absent
‘exceptions’ that the brief was directed toward supporting.” (CP Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16)
(emphasis in the original). Essentially, Charging Party interprets Section 1200.140(a)(3) to apply
only when a party elects to file exceptions and then files more exceptions in a supporting brief
because, as Charging Party asserts, “some exceptions may not need extensive argument and therefore
would not require a party to duplicate an ‘exception’ in an ‘exception’ document and in a brief.” (CP
1 On April 28, 2025, Charging Party filed an unopposed motion for a 30-day extension of time, which the Board’s General
Counsel granted, asserting the very same reasons he now claims require a variance from the Board’s Rules. It is unclear
why, and Charging Party offers no further explanation, Charging Party did not also ask for leave to file a brief in excess
of 50 pages or for clarification of the rules.
6

Resp. to Mtn. to Strike, ¶ 16) (emphasis in the original). This interpretation, however, is at odds with
Section 1200.135(b)(2), which allows parties to state the grounds in support of its exceptions in a
“supporting brief” subject to the constraints stated in Section 1200.135(b)(3), chief among them
being the constraint that “Any brief in support of exceptions shall be confined to the subjects raised
in the exceptions.” 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2) and (b)(3) (emphasis added). Because
Section 1200.135(b)(2) immediately precedes Section 1200.135(b)(3), Section 1200.135(b)(3) can
only be read to mean that if a party submits exceptions and elects to justify those exceptions in a
brief, that brief must only discuss those exceptions and cannot assert additional exceptions.
We strike the entirety of both Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting Brief in large
part because we grant Charging Party’s Motion for Variance and Leave to the extent Charging Party
may re-file his exceptions and brief in support as a single document representing “Charging Party’s
Exceptions and Brief in Support of Exceptions with Request for Oral Argument,” as stated in his
motion.
The criteria we use in considering a request for variances are provided in Section 1200.160 of
the Board’s Rules and are as follows:
a) the provision from which the variance is granted is not statutorily mandated;
b) no party will be injured by the granting of the variance; and
c) the rule from which the variance is granted would, in the particular case, be
unreasonable or unnecessarily burdensome.
80 Ill. Adm. Code §1200.160. The decision to grant a variance pursuant to the above criteria is made
at our discretion. Wood Dale Fire Prot. Dist. v. Ill. Labor Relations Bd., State Panel, 395 Ill. App. 3d
523, 530 (2d Dist. 2009) (holding that granting a variance under Board’s rules is left to Board’s
discretion, unless such decision is arbitrary or capricious); see also State of Ill., Dep’t of Cent. Mgmt.
Servs., 25 PERI 31 (IL LRB-SP Gen Counsel Order 2009), rev’d sub nom in State of Ill., Dep’t of
7

Central Mgmt. Servs. v. Ill. Labor Relations Bd., State Panel, et al., 26 PERI ¶ 77 (4th Dist. Rule 23
Order) (reversed and remanded for consideration of the merits of exceptions).
Applying the above criteria to this case, we find all three criteria satisfied. The 50-page
limitation set forth Section 1200.140.(b) and the 30-day timeframe for filing exceptions to a
recommended decision and order in unfair labor practice proceedings set forth in Section
1200.135(b)(1)(B) are not statutorily mandated; Respondent would not be prejudiced by allowing the
appeal because even if the Board were to allow the late filing, Respondent still would have the
opportunity to respond to the exceptions; and strictly adhering to the timeframe could be construed
as unreasonable and unduly burdensome in this particular case considering that Charging Party did
timely file exceptions, albeit incorrectly, and should not have to suffer the consequence of waiving
Board review of the RDO due to his attorney’s incorrect interpretation of the Board’s Rules.
To address Respondent’s concern regarding the need to seek leave to file a response in excess
of 50 pages, we proactively grant such leave in addition to resetting the due date for Respondent to
respond to Charging Party’s re-filed exceptions and brief in support. In addition, our resetting the
due date to respond to Charging Party’s re-filed exceptions does not change the due date, July 25,
2025, for Charging Party to respond to Respondent’s exceptions.
For the reasons set forth above, we strike Charging Party’s Exceptions and Supporting Brief
but grant the requested variance and allow Charging Party to re-file within 5 days of service of the
our Decision and Order its exceptions and brief in support as a single document representing
“Charging Party’s Exceptions and Brief in Support of Exceptions with Request for Oral Argument,”
as stated in his motion, not to exceed 60 pages exclusive of certificate of service. Charging Party’s
filing must otherwise comply with Section 1200.140(b) of the Board’s Rules. In addition, we grant
Respondent leave to file its response in excess of 50 pages and such response is due within 15 days
of service of Charging Party’s re-filed exceptions.

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On April 16, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Joseph Moy issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) finding Respondent Chief Judge of the Circuit Court
of Cook County (“Employer”) in default and concluding that Respondent violated Sections
10(a)(1) and 10(a)(2) and, derivatively, 10(a)(1) of the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act, (“Act),
5 ILCS 315/1 et seq. The Employer timely filed exceptions to the ALJ’s recommendations
contained in the RDO. Charging Party did not file a response to the appeal.1 After reviewing the
RDO, the record, and the Employer’s exceptions, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations contained
in the RDO but modify the remedy, as discussed below.
Charging Party Dorothy Ward filed the underlying unfair labor practice charge on
November 27, 2024, alleging that the Employer’s actions violated Section 10(a) of the Act when
it interfered with the exercise of Charging Party’s Weingarten rights and then retaliated against
1 Charging Party submitted an email to the Board’s General Counsel asking about the next steps in the proceedings.
Although she included assertions regarding union representation at meetings and retaliation for participating in
protected activity, she did not specifically respond to the Employer’s exceptions.
1

her for asserting those rights. The charge was investigated, and a Complaint for Hearing
(“Complaint”) issued pursuant to Section 1220.40 of the Board’s Rules and Regulations
(“Rules”). According to the Complaint, Charging Party is employed by Respondent in the title
of Mediator or “Conciliator Counselor” and is a member of the bargaining unit represented by
the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, Council 31 (“Union”).
During the relevant time period, Charging Party served as a steward for the Union.
The Complaint details communications and actions occurring during the period October
8, 2024 through November 14, 2024. It alleges that the Employer denied Charging Party’s request
for a Union representative during an October 18, 2024 investigatory meeting and issued her a
verbal reprimand for insubordination related to that meeting in violation of Section 10(a)(1) of
the Act. The Complaint further alleges that the Employer retaliated against Charging Party in
violation of Section 10(a)(2) and (1) of the Act.
The ALJ’s conclusion that the Employer violated the Act was based on finding it in
default for its failure to answer the Complaint within the 15-day timeframe set forth in Section
1220.40(b) of the Rules. The ALJ observed that the Complaint was served on the Employer on
February 14, 2025, by electronic mail to its counsel, Vincent Waller, and contained the following
statement:
RESPONDENT IS HEREBY NOTIFIED that within 15 days after
service of the complaint upon it, pursuant to Section 1220.40(b) of the Board’s
Rules and Regulations, 80 Ill. Admin. Code §§1200-1300, it must file an answer
to this complaint with Joseph Moy, at the Illinois Labor Relations Board, 160
North LaSalle Street, Suite S-400, Chicago, Illinois 60601, or electronically at
ILRB.Filing@Illinois.gov in accordance with Section 1200.5 of the Board’s
Rules and Regulations. Respondent must serve a copy of the answer upon
Charging Party. Please note that the Board’s Rules and Regulations do not allow
electronic service of the Answer upon Charging Party. Said answer shall
include an express admission, denial, or explanation of each and every
2

allegation of this complaint. Failure to specifically respond to an allegation shall
be deemed an affirmative admission of the facts or conclusions alleged in the
allegation. Failure to timely file an answer shall be deemed to be an admission
of all material facts or legal conclusions alleged and a waiver of hearing. The
filing of any motion or other pleading will not stay the time for filing an answer.
He observed that under Section 1220.40(b) of the Rules, the Employer was required to
file an answer to the Complaint, no later than March 3, 2025, but failed to do so by that date.
Consequently, on March 14, 2025, the ALJ issued an Order to Show Cause (“Order”) to the
Employer as to why it should not be held in default for failing to answer the complaint within the
15-day timeframe. In response to the Order, the Employer’s counsel attached a “Response to
Charging Party’s Complaint” that he claims was timely filed when it was submitted to the Board
agent investigating the charge (“Investigator”) on December 2024, but did not also submit it to
ILRB.Filing@Illinois.gov.
Construing the Employer’s response to the Order as a request for leave to file a late answer
to the Complaint, the ALJ denied the request. Citing Board and court precedent, the ALJ observed
that that the Employer’s stated reasons for failing to answer the Complaint amounted to attorney
inattention or negligence and did not constitute the “extraordinary circumstances” needed to allow
a late filing under Section 1220.40(b)(4) of the Board’s Rules. Furthermore, although the
Employer did not request a variance from the Rules, the ALJ determined that the criteria for
granting a variance could not be satisfied under these circumstances.
As a result, the ALJ found that the Employer defaulted and waived its right to a hearing
by failing to answer the Complaint within the prescribed 15-day period set forth in Section
1220.40(b) of the Board’s Rules. And because the Employer failed to answer the Complaint
within the allotted time, the ALJ found that pursuant to Section 1220.40(b)(3) of the Rules, the
Employer admitted all material facts and legal conclusions alleged in the Complaint and
3

determined that the Employer committed the unfair labor practices as alleged. The ALJ then
concluded that the Employer violated Section 10(a)(1) and 10(a)(2) and, derivatively, 10(a)(1)
of the Act and recommended that the Employer be ordered to cease and desist engaging in unfair
labor practices, post notice of the violation, and notify the Board of the steps it has taken to
comply with the order. We note, however, that the ALJ inadvertently omitted rescission and
removal of the verbal reprimand given to Charging Party for insubordination as a remedy.
Because the Employer failed to answer the Complaint, it has admitted the conclusion that it
retaliated against Charging Party by issuing a verbal reprimand to her, forming the basis for the
Section 10(a)(2) violation. As such, to make the Charging Party whole, we modify the remedy
to include the rescission of the verbal reprimand and its removal from Charging Party’s record.
The Employer filed four exceptions and a supporting brief and contends that:
1. The material facts alleged in the complaint and deemed admit-
ted do not support, and in fact, contradict the conclusions of law
in Section IV of the RDO[;]
2. The RDO errs in disregarding “other grounds traditionally re-
lied upon for equitable relief from judgments[”;]
3. The RDO errs in construing Section 1200.160 as the exclusive
mechanism for exercising discretion[; and]
4. Deeming the material facts and conclusions of law alleged in
the complaint admitted is an abuse of discretion.
The Employer contends that the ALJ erred by failing to exercise discretion and excuse
the failure to answer the Complaint as required by the Rules. Section 1200.160 of the Rules
allows the Board to grant a variance from the Rules so long as certain criteria are met:
a) the provision from which the variance is granted is not
statutorily mandated;
b) no party will be injured by the granting of the variance; and
c) the rule from which the variance is granted would, in the
particular case, be unreasonable or unnecessarily burdensome.
80 Ill. Adm. Code §1200.160. The Employer, however, has not satisfied the third criterion.
4

In seeking relief from application of the Rules in the answering of complaints, the
Employer mainly relies on the Illinois Appellate Court’s decision in Cook Cnty State’s Attorney
v. Ill. State Labor Relations Bd., et al., 292 Ill. App. 3d 1 (1st Dist. 1997) to support its
contentions. The Employer contends that, as in Cook Cnty State’s Attorney, its response to the
underlying unfair labor practice charge submitted to the Investigator demonstrates that the
Employer has a meritorious defense and that there are mitigating circumstances sufficient to
excuse its failure to answer the Complaint within the 15-day timeframe. The Employer also
questions whether the Board has considered its response submitted to the Investigator and seeks
variance from the Rules to allow additional time to “file a response to the complaint and/or [an]
opportunity for a hearing in this matter. The Employer also points to Section 1220.40(b)(4),
asserting that there are extraordinary circumstances sufficient to excuse its counsel’s neglect.
The Employer’s contentions are unavailing. The Employer’s reliance on Cook Cnty.
State’s Attorney in seeking to excuse its failure to answer the Complaint is unpersuasive because
that case is readily distinguishable. In Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney, the court found that the
Board abused its discretion by failing to grant a variance and accept the State’s Attorney answer
which the court found was filed only three hours late and would have been timely filed had the
State’s attorney mailed its answer. Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney, 292 Ill. App. 3d at 13 (finding
that “[i]n this case, the answer was filed approximately 3 hours late. Had the State’s Attorney
mailed its answer on December 12, 1995, [the fifteenth day], it would have been deemed
timely.”).
Here, the Employer did not, and still has not, filed an answer to the Complaint, much less
filed one within the brief time period at issue in Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney. Instead, applicable
here is the court’s decision in Wood Dale Fire Protection Dist. v. Ill. Labor Relations Bd., et al.,
5

395 Ill. App. 3d 523 (2nd Dist. 2009), which involves facts more closely resembling the facts in
this case. In Wood Dale Fire Protection Dist., the court upheld the Board’s denial of a variance
where the respondent “waited 28 days after the deadline to file an answer, and, even then, after
it had been alerted to its mistake, did not request a variance for another 24 days.” Wood Dale
Fire Protection Dist., 395 Ill. App. 3d at 532. The court also observed that the respondent only
cited its attorney’s mistake for the delay and offer no explanation for the additional delay in
requesting a variance. Id. The court found that such mitigating circumstances were “far less
compelling than those presented in Cook County State’s Attorney and the delay was far more
than the three hours presented in filed Cook County State’s Attorney.” Id. at 533. Notably, the
respondent in Wood Dale Fire Protection Dist., eventually filed an answer.
But that is not the case here. In response to the ALJ’s Order, the Employer asserted that
its counsel timely filed a “Response to the Charging Party’s Complaint” in December of 2024
but neglected to copy ILRB.Filing@Illinois.gov. The Employer also attached the “Response to
the Charging Party’s Complaint” to its response to the Order. The Response to the Charging
Party’s Complaint, however, is clearly not an answer to the Complaint. The Employer admittedly
submitted a position statement to the Investigator in December 2024, over two months before the
Complaint issued in February 2025. The Board, through its agents, the Investigator and
Executive Director, considered the Employer’s response to the charge submitted in December
when investigating the charge and issuing the Complaint pursuant to Section 1220.40(a) of the
Rules. 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1220.40(a). The submission of the position statement in response to
the Order, however, does not transform the position statement into an answer to the Complaint.
Section 1220.40(b) requires a respondent to admit, deny, or explain each allegation or issue of
the complaint and to serve a copy of its answer on the Charging Party. The document that the
6

Employer submitted in response to the ALJ’s Order does not comport with the requirements of
Section 1220.40(b) of the Board’s Rules. It does not answer every allegation of the Complaint
nor is there any evidence or contention that the Employer served this document on the Charging
Party. Thus, the document the Employer filed in response to the Order cannot be deemed an
answer to the Complaint.
On exceptions, the Employer attributes its failure to file an answer to its counsel’s
negligence, asserting that mitigating circumstances exist to justify a variance. The Employer’s
counsel asserts that he missed the email attaching the Complaint “due to a deluge of forwarded
emails coming from the Director level employee’s email account” and was out of the office when
he received the ALJ’s Order which he “mistakenly believed” was prompted by his failure to send
its position statement to the Board’s electronic filing address in addition to the Investigator.
Although the ALJ construed its response to the Order as requesting leave to file a late answer,
the Employer did not seek leave to file an answer until now. Notably, the Employer does not
seek leave to file an answer to the Complaint instanter. Rather, the Employer merely seeks a
variance from the Rules for an unquantified amount of time to file an answer, without explanation
for the further delay.
Moreover, the Employer contends that we should grant a variance based on the existence
of similar mitigating circumstances—burden on the taxpayer and conflict with the efficient
operations of the Office of the Chief Judge—that the court in Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney found
noteworthy. In reversing the Board’s refusal to accept a late answer or a variance, the court in
Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney took note of the State’s Attorney’s reasons for discharging the
employee and found the reinstatement of an employee who was fired for neglecting her duties as
a victim specialist, to be a burden on the taxpayer and at odds with the State’s Attorney’s mission
7

in excusing the three-hour delay in the filing of the answer. Cook Cnty. State’s Attorney 292 Ill.
App. 3d at 12.
Here, the Employer does not explain how the ALJ’s recommended remedy, a notice
posting, presents a burden to taxpayers or interferes with the Employer’s mission. Moreover,
even though we have modified the recommended remedy to include the rescission and removal
of the verbal reprimand for failing to attend a meeting, it is difficult to see how requiring the
Employer to do so would present a burden to the taxpayers or conflict with the Employer’s
mission.
Finally, the Employer’s primary contention that the Complaint fails to state a claim is
meritless. The Employer has not answered each and every allegation and issue stated in the
Complaint and as a result, all of the Complaint’s factual allegations and legal conclusions are
deemed admitted. 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1220.40(b)(3). Moreover, the Employer does not seek a
variance from that section, and we decline to do so on our own motion.
For the above reasons, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations contained in the RDO,
subject to the modification to the remedy as described above.
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that the Employer, its officers and agents, shall:
1) Cease and desist from:
a. Interfering with, restraining, or coercing the Charging Party in the exercise of her
rights by the Act when the Charging Party requests for a Union representative
during investigatory meetings.
b. Retaliating against the Charging Party for protected concerted activity of
requesting a Union representative attend the meeting with her and her supervisors.
c. Retaliating against the Charging Party to discourage membership in or support for
the Union.
d. In any like or related manner, interfering with, restraining or coercing its employees
in the exercise of the rights guaranteed them in the Act.
8

2) Take the following affirmative action necessary to effectuate the policies of the Act.
a. Make Charging Party whole by rescinding the verbal reprimand issued on
November 14, 2024, to Charging Party for insubordination and removing the same
from Charging Party’s employment records.
b. Post, at all places where notices to employees are normally posted, copies of the
Notice attached to this document. Copies of this Notice shall be posted, after being
duly signed, in conspicuous places, and be maintained for a period of 60
consecutive days. The Respondent will take reasonable efforts to ensure that the
notices are not altered, defaced or covered by any other material.
c. Notify the Board in writing, within 20 days from the date of this Decision, of the
steps the Respondent has taken to comply with this order.

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On April 16, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Donald Anderson issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) concluding that Respondent Chicago Transit Authority
(“CTA” or “Employer”) did not engage in unfair labor practices in violation of Section 10(a) of the
Illinois Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., as alleged by Charging Party Erek
Slater. The Charging Party and Respondent each filed exceptions and responses to each other’s
exceptions. Upon review and consideration of the record, the RDO, and the parties’ respective
exceptions and responses, and briefs in support, we reject the parties’ exceptions and adopt the RDO
as discussed below.
Background and Summary of RDO
During the relevant time period, Charging Party was employed by Respondent as a bus
operator working out of Respondent’s North Park Garage and a member of the bargaining unit
represented by the Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 241 (“Union”). Charging Party was also a
part-time member of the Union’s Executive Board. The instant matter involves incidents that took
place during the period May 31 through June 5, 2020, that lead to Charging Party’s termination from
employment. As part of its response to the civil unrest in the aftermath of the death of George Floyd,
1

the City of Chicago requested assistance from Respondent to transport police officers. Respondent
agreed to transport police officers to and from a staging area but did not agree to transport detainees.
Charging Party alleges that Respondent unlawfully discharged him for his conduct on May
31 and June 3, 2020. He alleges that on May 31, 2020, he engaged in protected, concerted activity
when he went to an area outside Respondent’s North Park Garage that was not an area of CTA
operations to read part of a statement from the President of the Amalgamated Transit Union’s
International and discuss the implications of transporting police officers during civil unrest.
Charging Party further asserted that Jeffrey Smith, a CTA Senior Manager, approached Charging
Party and demanded that Charging Party stop the discussion, insulted Charging Party, threatened to
remove Charging Party from service, and called the police. Respondent contends that on May 31,
2020, Smith overheard Charging Party tell other bus operators to refuse to drive buses transporting
police officers. When Smith asked Charging Party to leave the property, Charging Party refused to
leave and continued to tell bus operators to refuse to operate the police shuttles.
On June 3, 2020, Charging Party arrived at the North Park Garage and informed Smith that
Charging Party was there to work the pick. Because Smith had been told by Keith Hill, President of
the Union, that Beseemah Dear-Townsend, Union steward for the North Park Garage, would be
working the pick, Smith called Hill who, according to Smith, confirmed that Dear-Townsend was
assigned to work the pick, not Charging Party. When Smith left his office to talk to Charging Party,
he saw that Charging Party was blocking the doorway between CTA Business Manager Lachowicz’s
office and the clerk’s office and asked him to move away from the doorway. Charging Party refused
to leave at first but later left the office area and went to the Union table in the pick area.
The ALJ found that Charging Party failed to establish that Respondent unlawfully discharged
him in violation of Section 10(a)(1) and (a)(2) of the Act. Applying the burden-shifting analysis set
forth by the Illinois Supreme Court in City of Burbank, the ALJ determined that Charging Party
2

failed to establish a prima facie case for retaliation under Section 10(a)(1) of the Act because
Charging Party’s conduct on May 31, 2020, i.e., promoting a partial strike or work stoppage, did not
constitute protected, concerted activity. Based on his credibility determinations, the ALJ found that
on May 31, 2020, Charging Party was advocating for a partial strike/work stoppage, which the ALJ
concluded was not concerted activity because Charging Party failed to establish that he was acting
on the authority of other employees. The ALJ also found this activity was not protected because it
solicited and induced other employees to refuse to work.
The ALJ next found that Charging Party’s reading of the statement from the President of
ATU’s International (“International”) on May 31, 2020, and Charging Party’s working of the pick
on June 3, 2020, constituted union activity but determined that Charging Party failed to establish that
Respondent bore any anti-union animus toward the Union or towards Charging Party’s union
activities.
Parties’ Exceptions and Respective Responses
Charging Party’s Exceptions
Charging Party filed 40 separate exceptions to the RDO. These exceptions generally fall into
two categories: (1) Exceptions to the ALJ’s credibility determinations, factual findings, and
evaluation of evidence (Exceptions 1-16 and 29-40); and (2) Exceptions to the ALJ’s findings related
to the applicable law and analysis, (Exceptions 17-28).
Exceptions to ALJ’s Credibility Determinations, Factual Findings, and
Evaluation of Evidence
Charging Party filed 28 exceptions challenging the ALJ’s findings of fact most, of which
were based on the ALJ’s credibility determinations. Four of those exceptions, Exceptions 14, 16, 37,
& 38, do not state the grounds in support of the exceptions and/or do not identify citations to the
records or cite legal authority as required by Section 1200.135(b)(2) of the Board’s Rules and
3

Regulations.1 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2). As such, we disregard these exceptions pursuant
to that rule.
We find the remainder of Charging Party’s exceptions to the ALJ’s credibility determinations
(Exceptions 1-13, 15, and 29-35) unpersuasive, and accept the ALJ’s determinations. The Board has
long held that credibility determinations are within the province of the administrative law judge who
had the opportunity to observe the witnesses’ testimony and demeanor. Chicago Transit Authority,
16 PERI ¶ 3021 (IL LLRB 2000). As such, we will not overturn an ALJ's credibility determination
unless they are clearly and demonstrably incorrect. County of Cook and Sheriff of Cook County
(Malone-Cole), 39 PERI ¶ 3 (IL LRB-LP 2022); Chicago Transit Authority, 16 PERI ¶ 3021 (IL
LLRB 2000); City of Chicago (Fire Department), 12 PERI ¶ 3022 (IL LLRB 1996).
Here, Charging Party has not demonstrated that the ALJ’s credibility determinations are
clearly incorrect, for the record lends support to the ALJ’s credibility determinations. As the ALJ
recognized, unfair labor practice matters often involve differing version of events. As reflected in
Charging Party's testimony and that of Smith, Hill, Dear-Townsend, and/or other witnesses, the
instant matter is no exception, thereby raising the question of which version of events was more
credible. The ALJ answered that question by finding Respondent’s version of events more credible.
He found Smith’s testimony credible despite Charging Party’s assertions to the contrary, basing his
credibility determinations on context, specific occurrences and items of testimony, demeanor, and
the fact that Smith was no longer employed by Respondent when he testified at the hearing. The
1 Section 1200.135(b)(2) states in relevant part:
Exceptions . . . shall specifically set forth the questions of procedure, fact, law or policy to which exception
is taken, shall identify that part of the Administrative Law Judge's recommended decision and order to which
objection is made, and shall state the grounds for the exceptions and shall include the citation of authorities
and citations to the record unless set forth in a supporting brief. . . . Any exception that fails to comply with
the foregoing requirements may be disregarded.
80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2) (emphasis added).
4

ALJ also found that Smith’s testimony was corroborated by the testimony of Dear-Townsend and
Hill, which the ALJ found, on whole, to be credible.
In contrast, the ALJ observed that Charging Party’s version of events relied primarily on his
own testimony which was not corroborated by the witnesses that Charging Party called to testify at
the hearing. The ALJ found that most of the witnesses that Charging Party called were not shown to
have been in a position to observe any of the conduct at issue sufficient to corroborate Charging
Party’s testimony. The ALJ further observed that the only one of Charging Party’s witnesses who
did observe at least part of the events in question was Juan Alvarado, but the ALJ found that
Alvarado’s testimony did not sufficiently corroborate Charging Party’s testimony.
Moreover, a review of the record, specifically the portions of the record identified in Charging
Party’s exceptions brief, fail to demonstrate that the ALJ's credibility determinations were clearly
incorrect. For example, Charging Party’s Exception 15 challenges the ALJ’s findings related to Juan
Alvarado’s testimony appearing on page 41 of the RDO. The ALJ stated that Alvarado “testified
that he saw Slater talking with 10-15 operators in the picnic area, that a manager (presumably Smith)
came out and told Slater that he was not supposed to be talking to the operators, that Slater and the
manager got into an argument, with flailing arms and screaming, that he heard that ‘they’ were trying
to organize a work stoppage or wildcat, and that he was not sure if ‘he did or didn’t.’” (RDO, p. 41).
Charging Party contends that the ALJ inaccurately stated Alvarado’s testimony. Charging Party
identifies the actual statement as “You know what, I heard that they were trying to say that he was
trying to do that, but I am not sure if he did or he didn’t.” (Tr. Vol.1, p. 309: 13-15). Charging Party
further contends that Alvarado testified that he did not observe any work stoppage organization,
citing Alvarado’s testimony at (Tr. Vo1. 1, p. 309:18-19). Charging Party claims that contrary to the
ALJ’s findings, these pages corroborate Charging Party’s testimony that he was not promoting a
work stoppage.
5

The portion of Alvarado’s testimony on which Charging Party relies, however, does not
demonstrate that the ALJ’s assessment of Alvarado’s testimony was incorrect. Although the ALJ
did not state word for word that portion of Alvarado’s testimony identified by Charging Party, the
rest of the ALJ’s statement, that Alvarado testified that he saw Charging Party and Smith arguing,
arms flailing, and that he was not sure whether Charging Party “did or didn’t” advocate for a work
stoppage, finds support in the preceding pages, (Tr. Vol. 1, pp. 306-08), and in the pages following
those identified by Charging Party (Tr. Vol. 1, pp. 312-14). We find the three remaining exceptions,
Exceptions 36, 39, and 40, likewise without merit.
Exceptions to ALJ’s Legal Analysis
We find Charging Party’s exceptions to the ALJ’s legal analysis, Exceptions 17-28,
unpersuasive. As stated above, the ALJ recommended dismissal based on finding the Respondent’s
version of the events of May 31, June1, and June 3, 2020, to be more credible than Charging Party’s
version, and the ALJ appropriately applied relevant Board precedent and caselaw to the facts that
conformed with the testimony he determined to be more credible. We find Charging Party’s
exceptions unpersuasive because they are rooted in the Charging Party’s version of events which the
ALJ did not find credible. For example, in Exception 27, Charging Party contends he was denied
due process because the ALJ failed to make any findings related to the allegation that the June 1,
2020 incident constituted a violation of Section 10(a)(1) of the Act, under an objective standard.
Charging Party contends that on June 1, 2020, he was talking to employees at lunch tables about
safety issues related to driving police shuttles when Smith came out of his office and ordered him to
stop, threatening to call the police if he did not stop. Charging Party contends that the ALJ failed to
address this allegation, ostensibly denying him due process.
This exception, however, is unavailing. First, as Respondent points out in its response,
Charging Party does not provide any legal authority that the failure to make such a finding denies a
6

party due process. The ALJ conducted 7 days of hearing, entertained several lengthy procedural
motions filed by Charging Party, and issued an RDO resolving the issue. It is unclear, and Charging
Party fails to explain, how Charging Party was denied due process. Although the ALJ did not
specifically address the June 1, 2020, incident under the Section 10(a)(1) objective standard, we find
that he did not do so because he credited Smith’s version of events.
The exceptions that contend that the ALJ erred in applying, failing to apply, or misapplying
specific cases are also unpersuasive. Charging Party’s contentions fail to undermine the ALJ’s
analyses, for the ALJ correctly applied the relevant Board cases and caselaw. Although NLRB cases
are persuasive authority, they are not controlling precedent for the Board and thus, the ALJ was not
obligated to apply the NLRB cases that Charging Party contends should have been considered in the
ALJ’s analysis. Moreover, in Exception 23, Charging Party contends that the ALJ incorrectly relied
on Electronic Data Systems, 331 NLRB 343 (2020), because the NLRB overruled that case in Ohio
Bell Telephone Co., 370 N.L.R.B. No. 29 (2020), a case that Charging Party claims is now
controlling. But the NLRB in Ohio Bell Telephone Co., did not overrule Electronic Data Systems.
Rather, the NLRB in Ohio Bell Telephone Co., found Electronic Data Systems distinguishable on
the facts.
Charging Party’s Request for Oral Argument
We deny Charging Party’s request for oral argument pursuant to Section 1200.135(c) of the
Board’s Rules and Regulations. 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(c). Section 1200.135(c) of the
Board’s Rules and Regulations provides that “. . . [t]he Board shall grant or deny requests for oral
argument depending upon the significance, complexity and novelty of the issues.” Although length
and number of exceptions in this case may suggest otherwise, we find that the issues involved in this
case are neither significant, complex, nor novel.
7

Respondent’s Limited Exceptions
Respondent filed two exceptions related to the ALJ’s finding that Charging Party engaged in
union activity on May 31, 2025 and June 3, 2020. Respondent’s first exception disputes the ALJ’s
finding that Charging Party was engaged in union activity when he was, at least initially, at the garage
working the pick on that day but the record was not clear as to whether he was scheduled to work
that day. Respondent contends that both Smith and Hill testified that Charging Party was not assigned
to work the pick for the Union nor was scheduled to be at the garage for his regular work assignment,
and thus he was not engaging in legitimate union activity. Respondent’s contention does not
sufficiently undermine the ALJ’s finding that Charging Party was engaging in union activity on June
3, 2020. A review of the cited portions of Smith’s and Hill’s testimony supports the contention that
Charging Party was not assigned to work the pick for the Union or work for Respondent, but it is
undisputed that Charging Party was a member of the Executive Board and thus a union representative
and claimed to be there on Union business.
Respondent’s second exception also involves the ALJ’s finding regarding union activity and
is likewise unpersuasive. Respondent contends that the ALJ’s apparent finding that Charging Party
engaged in union activity on May 31, 2020, is incorrect. Respondent asserts that in analyzing the
Section 10(a)(2) claim, the ALJ assumed that Charging Party engaged in union activity by reading a
portion of the statement from the President of the Union’s International. Respondent contends this
is inconsistent with the ALJ’s finding that Charging Party’s activities on that day were not protected,
concerted activity. Respondent further asserts that such finding was based on the ALJ’s credibility
determination.
Respondent’s second exception fails to undermine the ALJ’s finding. The ALJ’s finding at
issue does not contradict his finding that Charging Party’s promotion of a partial strike on May 31,
2020, did not constitute protected, concerted activity. The allegations regarding the May 31, 2020,
8

incident involved two different activities: (1) the alleged reading of the statement from the President
of the International about safety issues surrounding driving police shuttles, and (2) the alleged
promotion of a partial strike/work stoppage. The ALJ appears to have focused on the partial strike
activity because that was the activity Respondent stated as the basis for Charging Party’s dismissal.
In sum, the ALJ’s findings, conclusions, and recommendations find support in the record and
applicable caselaw. Nothing in those exceptions undermines the ALJ’s findings and conclusions.
For the above reasons, we reject the parties’ exceptions as meritless and adopt the ALJ’s
recommendations for the reasons articulated in the RDO.

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On August 22, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed a charge filed by
Charging Party Latrice Moton on June 28, 2025. Charging Party was employed in the title
Veterans Certified Nursing Assistant by the State of Illinois, Department of Veteran’s Affairs
(“Employer”), and a member of the bargaining unit represented by Respondent American
Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees, Council 31, (“AFSCME”). The charge
alleges that Respondent engaged in unfair labor practices within the meaning of Section 10(b) of
the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., by failing to file a grievance
challenging Charging Party’s transfer, her placement on administrative leave, and her termination
from employment. The charge also alleged that Respondent gave her conflicting information
about whether Chief Union Steward Genara Gordon would continue to help her in light of the
Charging Party’s filing of the instant charge.
The Executive Director dismissed the charge on grounds the allegations failed to raise
issues warranting a hearing. Noting the intentional misconduct standard in duty of fair
1

representation cases set forth in Section 10(b)(1) of the Act, the Executive Director observed
that Charging Party failed to provide evidence indicating Respondent took any action against her
due to any bias or hostility towards Charging Party’s activities and/or status that would constitute
intentional misconduct or that would undermine a union’s considerable discretion in contract
interpretation and grievance handling. She also found little evidence that Gordon’s alleged lack
of assistance hindered Respondent’s representation of Charging Party. Finally, the Executive
Director observed that Respondent did file a grievance over Charging Party’s discharge, which
was pending at the time of the investigation.
Charging Party timely appealed the Executive Director’s dismissal; the Respondent did
not file a response. On appeal, Charging Party claims the Executive Director failed to consider
evidence that Charging Party contends is key to demonstrating Respondent’s intentional
misconduct. Charging Party includes with her appeal text message exchanges between Charging
Party and Union Representative Tramkia Robinson, emails she sent to Robinson, and explains
how such evidence undermines the Executive Director’s determinations. She claims that the text
messages included as Exhibit A to the appeal demonstrate the Chief Union Steward’s “refusal to
assist due to the pending claim” and that the text messages included as Exhibit C to the appeal
demonstrate the Respondent’s inconsistency and neglect. Charging Party also asserts that her
email to Robinson contains a “Statement of Facts for Grievance, citing unlawful discrimination
and CBA violations.”
Upon review of the dismissal order, the record, and Charging Party’s appeal, we find the
appeal without merit for it offers no viable basis to undermine the Executive Director’s grounds
for dismissal. Specifically, the appeal fails to provide or point to any evidence that Respondent
failed to file or pursue a grievance for Charging Party due to any bias or hostility toward Charging
2

Party’s status or activity. Moreover, the materials included with the appeal fail to undermine the
Executive Director’s findings or raise issues for hearing on the elements of intentional misconduct
needed to prevail in duty of fair representation cases. Finally, as the Executive Director found,
Respondent did file a grievance over Charging Party’s discharge. Accordingly, the Executive
Director correctly dismissed the charge on grounds that the available evidence failed to raise issues
of fact or law warranting a hearing on the allegations that the Respondent engaged in unlawful
activity in violation of Section 10(b)(1) of the Act.
For the above reasons, we affirm the dismissal of the charge for the reasons stated by the
Executive Director.
