DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On May 12, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed the unfair labor practice
charge filed by Charging Party Charles Friend on February 22, 2025. Charging Party is employed
by the Respondent, the State of Illinois Department of Transportation (“Employer” or “IDOT”) in
the job title Highway Maintainer and is a member of the bargaining unit represented by the
International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Local 916 (“Union”). The charge alleges that the
Respondent engaged in unfair labor practices within the meaning of Section 10(a) of the Illinois
Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., by interfering with Charging Party’s
steward duties and suspending him in retaliation for carrying out those duties. The charge also
alleged that Respondent retaliated against him for filing certain complaints with the Office of the
Executive Inspector General (“OEIG”).
At the center of the charge’s allegations are several incidents that took place in September
2024 at Respondent’s Decatur Maintenance Facility (“Facility”). Charging Party works as a
Highway Maintainer at the Facility and serves as a steward for the Union. On September 23,
1

2024, after confirming with Respondent’s Operation Supervisor, Jeff Wood, that under
Respondent’s current policy, former discharged employees are banned from Respondent’s
worksites, Charging Party informed Wood that an individual who Respondent had discharged in
2021, Krystal Rigdon, was present at the Facility as an employee of United Contractors Midwest
Paving (“UCMP”), one of the Respondent’s contractors, and wanted to know how Respondent
would resolve the matter. Charging Party later learned from the Union that Rigdon is not an active
Union member and has not been one since 2017.
Then on September 26, 2024, Charging Party was involved in several verbal exchanges
involving Rigdon, UCMP Supervisor Kim Wierman, and several other employees of the
Respondent, i.e., Construction Engineer Robert Gruel, Highway Maintenance Lead Worker John
Brownlee, Highway Maintainer Roger Cox, and Highway Maintainer Garrett Wilcoxen. The
following is a summary of the exchanges:
Exchange #1—Charging Party informed Wierman that Rigdon
should not be on Respondent’s worksite because she was a previously
discharged employee and was not a member of the Union.
Exchange #2—Later, Gruel told Charging Party to cease
speaking to the contractor and then Brownlee told Charging Party to “get
to work.”
Exchange #3—Sometime after Exchange #1 and #2, Charging
Party saw Rigdon and commented that she was still on premises after
being given the opportunity to leave. Rigdon responded with expletive
directed at Charging Party. Wierman approached and instructed Rigdon
to return to her vehicle. After Rigdon left, Charging Party exchanged
words with Wierman. Then sometime after that, Charging Party entered
into a separate verbal exchange with Cox.
Exchange #4—Sometime later, Charging Party and Cox engaged
in another verbal exchange over Charging Party’s conduct. Cox told
Charging Party that Charging Party did not understand his role as
steward and was “espousing authority” that Charging Party did not have.
Cox then informed Charging Party that he contacted Union business
2

agent Dave Rush to request that another Union representative be
assigned to the worksite.
Exchange #5—Charging Party entered into a verbal exchange
with another co-worker, Garrett Wilcoxen, who told Charging Party that
his conduct was not appropriate and could lead to the Charging Party’s
discharge. Charging Party replied that Wilcoxen “just wanted a pansy
for a union steward.”
On October 26, 2026, Charging Party met with a Union representative and the Respondent
to discuss the workplace violations that Charging Party had allegedly committed on September 16,
2024. The alleged violative conduct included impeding business operations, harassing and arguing
with UCMP workers as well as arguing with fellow employees, which resulted in a traffic backup
out of the yard and on to the street. Respondent further alleged that Charging Party threatened to
have another employee discharged when he stated that he would see him on the unemployment
line. Charging Party denied the allegations and claimed that he believed Rigdon’s presence at the
worksite posed a safety risk, a belief he claimed was supported by Rigdon’s failure to take a drug
test in 2021. On November 7, 2024, Charging Party received a 5-day suspension.
The Executive Director dismissed the charge on grounds that the allegations failed to raise
issues warranting a hearing. The Executive Director construed the charge as alleging retaliation
for participation in protected activity and applied the burden-shifting analysis set forth by the
Illinois Supreme Court in City of Burbank v. Illinois State Labor Relations Board, 128 Ill.2d 335,
345 (1989). Noting the elements of the prima facie case for retaliation under Section 10(a)(1)
and (a)(2), she dismissed the charge’s allegations because the available evidence failed to indicate
that Respondent suspended Charging Party because he participated in union activity, or any
concerted activity protected by the Act. The Executive Director further determined that the
evidence failed to demonstrate that Charging Party’s activity triggering Charging Party’s
3

suspension is protected by the Act or that Respondent prevented or hindered Charging Party in
engaging in protected union activity.
Moreover, the Executive Director found that the available evidence failed to demonstrate
a causal connection between Charging Party’s protected union activity and the imposition of a 5-
day suspension against him. The Executive Director noted the lack of evidence indicating that
the Respondent bore any animus, anti-union or otherwise, towards Charging Party’s participation
in protected activity, noting that the available evidence indicated that Respondent was motivated
by Charging Party’s conduct towards his fellow co-workers and the employees of Respondent’s
contractors. Lastly, the Executive Director determined that the Board lacks jurisdiction over
claims of retaliation based on Charging Party’s OEIG complaints against Wood.
Charging Party timely appealed the dismissal order. Respondent did not file a response.
Upon review of the dismissal order, the record, and Charging Party’s appeal, we find the appeal
without merit and sustain the Executive Director’s dismissal order, subject to modification as
discussed below.
On appeal, Charging Party primarily disputes the Executive Director’s determinations
that Respondent did not interfere with Charging Party’s steward activities. Specifically,
Charging Party asserts that he filed the charge “because my immediate supervisor, Jeff Wood
(OS1), who was not at the Decatur Facility on September [26], 2024, so, he instructed the Facility
Lead Worker John Brownlee, and the contractor engineer, Robert [Gruel], to interfere with a
Union Steward[‘s] protected activities.” Charging Party also takes issue with the Executive
Director’s characterization of his claim as one of discrimination and contends that his was only
obligated to demonstrate in his charge “that the respondent [sic] interfered in my Protected
Activities, and that they retaliated against me for doing so. . . . I don’t believe that I indicated at
4

any time with [the Board agent] that I was discriminated against, other than MAYBE JW
retaliated because I have filed OIEG [sic] complaints against him.” Charging Party further asserts
that his “concerns were for EVERYONE at the facility, not ‘singular’ as Mackins has stated.”
Charging Party also contends that he was denied due process and criticizes the length and
substance of the investigation conducted by Board agent, Tiara Mackins. Charging Party asserts
that he was denied due process because the Board agent “refused to hear from [his] witness,” a
former Vice President of the Union who could provide testimony in Charging Party’s defense
and affirm a steward’s right to ask for Union membership status.
We find Charging Party’s appeal to be meritless and thus affirm the dismissal of the
charge but modify the analysis to include a determination regarding Charging Party’s interference
claim and to address the portion of the dismissal regarding Charging Party’s OEIG complaint
against Wood.
Although the Executive Director found that the available evidence failed to support
Charging Party’s claim that Respondent interfered with Charging Party’s steward duties, i.e.,
asking about the union membership status of the contract employees at the Facility, the dismissal
order does not address interference with the rights guaranteed by the Act as an independent
violation of Section 10(a)(1). Section 10(a)(1) of the Act provides, in relevant part, that “it shall
be an unfair labor practice for an employer or its agents to interfere with, restrain or coerce public
employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in this Act.” 5 ILCS 315/10(a)(1). Section 6
of the Act broadly states that public employees have the right to join unions, to bargain
collectively and to “engage in other concerted activities not otherwise prohibited by law for the
purposes of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection, free from interference,
restraint or coercion.” 5 ILCS 315/6(a). In the absence of retaliation allegations, the Board
5

applies a reasonable employee test which considers whether the employer’s conduct, viewed
objectively from the standpoint of a reasonable employee, had a tendency to interfere with,
restrain or coerce the employee in the exercise of a right guaranteed by the Act. Clerk of the
Circuit Court, 7 PERI ¶ 2019 (IL SLRB 1991); Ill., Dep’t. of Cent. Mgmt. Servs. (Dept. of
Conservation), 2 PERI ¶ 2032 (IL SLRB 1986).
Applying the above principles, we find Charging Party’s contentions regarding the
Section 10(a)(1) interference claim unavailing. As the Executive Director correctly determined,
the available evidence fails to support Charging Party’s contentions that Respondent interfered
with his steward duties independent of his retaliation claim. And because the charge alleged
retaliation, as the Charging Party asserts in his appeal, the Executive Director applied the
analytical framework used for Section 10(a)(2) claims set forth by City of Burbank, to determine
whether a public employer took adverse action against an employee for participating in protected,
concerted activity in violation of Section 10(a)(1) and 10(a)(2) of the Act. City of Burbank, 128
Ill.2d at 345 (1989); Pace Suburban Bus Div. v. Ill Labor Rel. Bd., State Panel, 406 Ill. App. 3d
484, 494-95 (1st Dist. 2010) (applying the City of Burbank analysis to retaliation claims under
Section 10(a)(1) of the Act). Under such analysis as applied to Section 10(a)(1) retaliation
claims, a charging party must show that (1) the employee at issue was engaged in protected, union
activity; (2) the employer knew of his conduct, and (3) the employer took the adverse action
against him due to animus toward the protected, concerted activity. Pace Suburban Bus Div.,
406 Ill. App. 3d at 494-95.
The Executive Director applied the foregoing analysis and determined that the available
evidence failed to support allegations that the Respondent retaliated against the Charging Party
for performing his steward duties or engaging in any other protected activity in violation of
6

Section 10(a)(1) and 10(a)(2). Charging Party, however, does not provide any evidence or cogent
argument sufficient to undermine the Executive Director’s determinations regarding retaliation.
Instead, Charging Party merely asserts that the Respondent interfered with his right to ask about
the Union membership status of employees working for the Respondent’s contractors, without
explaining how Respondent has done so independent of the imposition of his 5-day suspension
underlying the charge’s retaliation allegations.
Charging Party’s contention that the Executive Director incorrectly found that his activities
did not involve a group concern is also without merit. An employee engages in concerted activity
when he or she acts, jointly or individually, on behalf of others or invokes a right under a
collective bargaining agreement, but not when the employee acts solely on his own behalf. See
Cnty. of Cook (Mgmt. Information Serv.), 11 PERI ¶ 3012 (IL LLRB 1995). All union activity
is concerted activity, but not all concerted activity is union activity. City of Elmhurst, 17
PERI ¶ 2040 (IL LRB-SP 2001); Vill. of Bensenville, 10 PERI ¶ 2009 (IL SLRB 1993).
The Executive Director found that Charging Party engaged in union activity on September 23 and
September 26, 2024, when he asked Wood about the Respondent’s policy banning discharged
employees at the Respondent’s worksite and when he inquired about the Union membership status
of contract employees. Thus, by definition, Charging Party’s union activity involved a group
concern.
Turning to the finding regarding OEIG complaints, although the Executive Director
correctly observes that the Board lacks authority over OEIG complaints, the Board does have
jurisdiction to enforce unfair labor practice charges involving the filing of an OEIG complaint as
protected, concerted activity. In this case, however, the available evidence does not support a
7

finding that Charging Party’s OEIG complaint constituted protected, concerted activity or that
Respondent took any action against the Charging Party because he filed an OEIG complaint.
We find that Charging Party’s contentions regarding due process and the conduct of the
investigation are also without merit. Section 11(a) of the Act provides that the Board or any agent
designated by the Board has the authority to investigate unfair labor charges, and that the Board
has the authority to issue complaints for hearing. 5 ILCS 315/11(a). Section 1220.40(a) of the
Board’s rules sets forth the investigatory process and delegates the authority to issue complaints
to the Board’s Executive Director. 80 Ill. Adm. Code §1220.40(a). The Board’s rules do not
include minimum requirements on the scope of the investigation the Board or its agents may
conduct to determine whether there are issues of law or fact sufficient to warrant the issuance of a
complaint. See 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1220.40(a). The rules place the responsibility on a charging
party to “submit to the Board or its agent all evidence relevant to or in support of the charge. The
evidence may include documents and affidavits.” 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1220.40(a)(1).
Here, a review of the investigatory record reveals that the Board agent conducted a
thorough investigation in which the Charging Party was afforded ample opportunity to provide
documents and information in support of his unfair labor practice charge. Charging Party contends
on appeal that he was denied due process because the investigator “refused” to consider testimony
from a former Vice President of Teamster Local 916, who Charging Party asserts “would be more
than happy to provide testimony in [his] defense, and concur with Unwritten practices of Shop
Stewards being afforded the right to ask for Union Status.” But a review of the investigatory
record reveals that the Charging Party provided the names of this witness on March 26, 2025, after
the March 13, 2024, deadline for the submission of information in support of the charge had
passed.
8

Moreover, although the dismissal order misstates the Charging Party’s job title and
identifies the wrong union, such errors were not material to the Executive Director’s analysis and
conclusions. Lastly, Charging Party’s criticisms of the length of the investigation are unfounded.
Charging Party asserts that the “ILRB has had this case for almost 9 months,” but the charge was
filed on February 22, 2025, initiating the investigation, and the Executive Director issued the
dismissal order on May 12, 2025, less than 3 months from the date the charge was filed.
For the above reasons, we affirm the dismissal of the charge for the reasons stated by the
Executive Director subject to modification as discussed above.

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On April 18, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed a charge filed by
Charging Party Reivis Barileau on February 9, 2025. Charging Party is a Human Rights
Investigator II with the Respondent Illinois Department of Human Rights (“Employer” or
“IDHR” ) and a member of the bargaining unit represented by the American Federation of State,
County, and Municipal Employees, Council 31 (“Union”). The charge alleges that the
Respondent engaged in unfair labor practices within the meaning of Section 10(a) of the Illinois
Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., by retaliating against her for
participating in protected, concerted activity and unilaterally changing workplace policy. After
receiving additional information from the Charging Party, the investigator assigned to the matter
amended the charge to allege violations of Section 10(a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(4) of the Act.
The Executive Director dismissed the amended charge on grounds the allegations failed
to raise issues for warranting a hearing. The Executive Director construed the charge as alleging
that the Respondent retaliated against the Charging Party by issuing multiple Corrective Action
1

Plans (“CAPs”) because she filed a complaint with the Office of the Executive Inspector General
(“OEIG”). Noting the elements of the prima facie case for retaliation under Section 10(a)(1) and
(a)(2), she dismissed such allegations because the available evidence failed to indicate that the
Charging Party’s OEIG complaint constituted protected, concerted activity. The Executive
Director further reasoned that even if the OEIG complaint could be considered protected,
concerted activity, there was no evidence that Respondent had knowledge of Charging Party’s
OEIG complaint before the OEIG referred the complaint to the Respondent on October 4, 2024.
The Executive Director then observed that even if Respondent had knowledge of the
OEIG complaint before October 4, 2024, the evidence failed to indicate a causal connection
between the filing of the OEIG complaint and the issuance of multiple CAPs to the Charging
Party. She determined that the Respondent had already issued four CAPs starting on May 15,
2024, and continuing through September 23, 2024, well before the OEIG referred the Charging
Party’s OEIG matter to the Respondent. The Executive Director also noted the lack of evidence
indicating that the Respondent bore any animus, anti-union or otherwise, towards Charging
Party’s participation in protected activity or treated Charging Party more harshly than other
similarly situated employees who did not file an OEIG complaint. Lastly, the Executive Director
dismissed Charging Party’s unilateral change allegations on the grounds that individual charging
parties lack standing to file charges under Section 10(a)(4) of the Act.
Charging Party timely appealed the Executive Director’s dismissal; the Respondent did
not file a response.
On appeal, Charging Party disputes the Executive Director’s determinations that the filing
of her OEIG complaint did not constitute protected, concerted activity and that the Respondent
lacked knowledge of Charging Party’s OEIG complaint. Charging Party further contends that
2

the Executive Director incorrectly required a showing of union animus as an element of the prima
facie case for retaliation and failed to conduct a full investigation of the charge. Moreover,
Charging Party concedes that unilateral change allegations may only be brought by the Union
but contends that the allegations involving the Respondent’s alleged changes to its remote work
policy should have been analyzed under Section 10(a)(1) as interference with public employee
rights under the Act.
Regarding concerted activity, Charging Party contends that the Executive Director
misconstrues concerted activity and asserts that “whistle-blower” filings and group grievances
are protected activity under the Act, citing Board decisions in City of Chi. (Conroy), 33 PERI ¶
51 (IL LRB-LP 2020) (Case No. L-CA-15-020); Oak Brook Park Dist., 31 PERI ¶ 193 (IL LRB-
SP 2015). Charging Party claims that her OEIG complaint was filed to seek relief for all
investigators and for “mutual aid or protection.” Charging Party further claims that the Board’s
decision in City of Decatur, 14 PERI ¶ 2004 (IL LRB-SP 1997) compels the crediting of “such
unrebutted documentary allegations at the dismissal stage.”
In support of her contentions regarding the Executive Director’s finding that the
Employer lacked knowledge of the OEIG complaint, Charging Party asserts that her May 20,
2024 email to Emily Spreng, Bret Harzman, and Pamela Hudson, announcing her intent to file a
complaint with the OEIG imputed knowledge of her OEIG complaint to the Employer. Charging
Party argues that such knowledge, coupled with timing, evidences that the Respondent treated
her more harshly than the employees that she listed in her appeal and referenced exhibits.
Upon review of the dismissal order, the record, and appeal, we affirm the dismissal of the
charge but with modification of the Executive Director’s analysis of the 10(a)(2) claims. The
Executive Director dismissed the Section 10(a)(2) allegations based in part on the lack of
3

evidence of union animus towards Charging Party’s protected activity. Charging Party contends
that the Executive Director erred by requiring evidence of union animus in dismissing her charge
because retaliation under Section 10(a)(1) does not require such a showing.1 There is some merit
to Charging Party’s contentions. See Pace Suburban Bus Div. of Reg’l Transp. Auth. v. Ill.
Labor Relations Bd., State Panel, 406 Ill. App. 3d 484, 494-95 (1st Dist. 2010) (finding an
employee can demonstrate the improper motive element of a prima facie case of retaliation under
Section 10(a)(1) by showing that the employer took action due to animus toward her participation
in protected activity).
Notwithstanding the above, Charging Party’s contentions regarding the Section 10(a)(1)
claims are unavailing. The Executive Director construed the charge as alleging that the
Respondent retaliated against Charging Party for filing an OEIG complaint concerning the CAPs
that she received and the conduct of her supervisors. Section 10(a)(1) of the Act provides, in
relevant part, that “it shall be an unfair labor practice for an employer or its agents to interfere
with, restrain or coerce public employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in this Act.” 5
ILCS 315/10(a)(1). Section 6 of the Act broadly states that public employees have the right to
join unions, to bargain collectively and to “engage in other concerted activities not otherwise
prohibited by law for the purposes of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection, free
from interference, restraint or coercion.” 5 ILCS 315/6(a).
Motivation of a public employer is relevant to a Section 10(a)(1) analysis where a charging
party alleges the employee at issue suffered an adverse employment action. See Pace Suburban
Bus Div., 406 Ill. App. 3d 484 at 494-95. In such cases, the Board applies the analytical
framework used for Section 10(a)(2) claims set forth by the Illinois Supreme Court in City of
1 Charging Party appears to have conceded the dismissal of any Section 10(a)(2) claim as she does not allege that the
Respondent bore any union animus in taking the alleged action against her.
4

Burbank v. Ill. State Labor Relations Bd., 128 Ill.2d 335, 345 (1989), to determine whether a
public employer took adverse action against an employee for an unlawful motive. Pace Suburban
Bus Div., 406 Ill. App. 3d at 495. Under this analysis as applied to Section 10(a)(1) retaliation
claims, a charging party must show that (1) the employee at issue was engaged in protected, union
activity; (2) the employer knew of his conduct, and (3) the employer took the adverse action
against him due to animus toward the protected, concerted activity. Pace Suburban Bus Div.,
406 Ill. App. 3d at 494-95.
The threshold issue in this case is whether by filing her complaint with the OEIG the Charging
Party was engaging in concerted activity. For individual employee actions to be considered
“concerted activity,” such actions must be undertaken “ with or on the other authority of” other
employees in furtherance of a group concern. See Oak Brook Park Dist., 31 PERI ¶ 193 ; City
of Decatur, 14 PERI ¶ 2004 ; Vill. of Bensenville, 10 PERI ¶ 2009 (IL SLRB 1993); see also
Schaumburg Sch. Dist. v. Ill. Educ. Labor Relations Bd., 247 Ill. App. 3d 439, 456-8 (1st Dist.
1993). An employee acting by herself without contacting other employees, even with the desire
to help the other employees, does not satisfy the concerted action requirement. See Oak Brook
Park Dist., 31 PERI ¶ 193 (“Concerted action cannot be imputed from the object of the action.”);
see also City of Decatur, 14 PERI ¶ 2004 ( the employee must be actually, not impliedly,
representing the views of other employees.”).
Here, the Executive Director correctly concluded that the filing of Charging Party’s OEIG
complaint did not constitute concerted activity, reasoning that the OEIG complaint expressed
Charging Party’s opinions about Respondent’s mismanagement of the department and that her
supervisors misapplied the 180-day timeline for IDHR investigators to complete their
assignments. Charging Party asserts that her OEIG complaint is concerted activity because she
5

filed the complaint on behalf of all IDHR investigators as a group concern. This assertion,
however, is insufficient to reverse dismissal. Although Charging Party claims she filed the
complaint on behalf of other investigators, she does not provide evidence, or even allege, that she
filed the OEIG complaint with or on the authority of the other investigators or that she agreed
with at least one other investigator to file a complaint with the OEIG over the matters included
in that complaint. See City of Decatur, 14 PERI ¶ 2004 (finding that to be concerted, at least
two employees must have “agreed to do something about their jointly held complaints”); see also
City of Waukegan, 24 PERI ¶ 77 (IL LRB-SP 2008) (no concerted protected activity found where
there was no evidence that the employee at issue was serving as a “spokesperson” for other
employees.).
Even if we were to find that Charging Party’s filing of the OEIG complaint constituted
protected, concerted activity, Charging Party fails to point to or provide evidence undermining the
Executive Director’s determinations regarding Respondent’s lack of knowledge of the OEIG
complaint and the lack of a causal connection between the filing of Charging Party’s OEIG
complaint and the alleged adverse actions.
The Executive Director found that the Respondent did not have knowledge of Charging
Party’s OEIG complaint until the OEIG referred the complaint to the Respondent on October 4
2024, after the Respondent had already begun issuing CAPs to the Charging Party. Charging Party
challenges this finding, contending that she informed the Respondent that she would be filing a
complaint with the OEIG in her May 20, 2024 email.
Assuming that Charging Party’s May 20, 2024 email satisfies the knowledge element of
the prima facie case, Charging Party’s arguments on appeal fail to undermine the Executive
Director’s determinations regarding the requisite causal connection between the filing of Charging
6

Party’s OEIG complaint and the issuance of CAPs to the Charging Party. Noting that causal
connection can be established by demonstrating that the Respondent treated Charging Party
disparately in comparison to other similarly situated employees, the Executive Director found that
contrary to the Charging Party’s claims, CAPs were issued to other investigators.
Referencing a “Full 16-row chart” submitted during the investigation in support of her
contention that she received disparate treatment, Charging Party points to five other investigators
who she claims had late cases but did not receive CAPs. A review of that chart, however, confirms
the Executive Director’s finding that other investigators who had late cases also received CAPs.
Without disparate treatment, only the timing of the alleged adverse action remains. But timing
alone is insufficient to establish a violation of the Act. See Sarah D. Culbertson Memorial Hosp.,
21 PERI ¶ 6 (IL LRB-SP 2005).
Turning to the unilateral change allegations, Charging Party contends that Respondent’s
unilateral changes to its remote work policy should be analyzed under Section 10(a)(1) as
interference with public employee rights under the Act. As stated above, Section 10(a)(1) of the
Act provides, in relevant part, that “it shall be an unfair labor practice for an employer or its
agents to interfere with, restrain or coerce public employees in the exercise of the rights
guaranteed in this Act.” 5 ILCS 315/10(a)(1). Section 6 of the Act broadly states that public
employees have the right to join unions, to bargain collectively and to “engage in other concerted
activities not otherwise prohibited by law for the purposes of collective bargaining or other mutual
aid or protection, free from interference, restraint or coercion.” 5 ILCS 315/6(a). In the absence
of retaliation allegations, the Board applies a reasonable employee test which considers whether
the employer’s conduct, viewed objectively from the standpoint of a reasonable employee, had a
tendency to interfere with, restrain or coerce the employee in the exercise of a right guaranteed
7

by the Act. Clerk of the Circuit Court, 7 PERI ¶ 2019 (IL SLRB 1991); State of Ill., Dep’t of
Cent. Mgmt. Servs. (Dep’t of Conserv.), 2 PERI ¶ 2032 (IL SLRB 1986).
Here, Charging Party’s contention that the loss of the ability to work remotely after
receiving three CAPs discourages employees from contesting CAPs raises issues for hearing on
Section 10(a)(1) violations are without merit. In this instance, we cannot find that contesting an
individual employee’s CAP is a public employee right guaranteed by the Act. It is not related to
the right to join a union or to bargain collectively, nor can it be viewed as engaging in concerted
activities for the purposes of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection. See 5 ILCS
315/6(a). Moreover, even if contesting CAPs could be considered a right guaranteed by the Act,
it is unclear how a reasonable employee would be discouraged from contesting CAPs because he
or she could lose remote work benefits after receiving three CAPs. Indeed, it would be more
likely that a reasonable employee would seek to challenge a CAP to avoid receiving three of them
and lose the remote work benefit.
Lastly, Charging Party’s contention that the Executive Director’s failure to conduct a full
investigation warrants reversal of the dismissal order is without merit. Section 11(a) of the Act
provides that the Board or any agent designated by the Board has the authority to investigate unfair
labor charges, and that the Board has the authority to issue complaints for hearing. 5 ILCS
315/11(a). Section 1220.40(a) of the Board’s rules sets forth the investigatory process and
delegates the authority to issue complaints to the Board’s Executive Director. 80 Ill. Adm. Code
§1220.40(a). The Board’s rules do not include minimum requirements on the scope of the
investigation that the Board or its agents must conduct to determine whether there are issues of
law or fact sufficient to warrant the issuance of a complaint. See id. The Board’s rules place the
responsibility on the charging party to “submit to the Board or its agent all evidence relevant to or
8

in support of the charge. The evidence may include documents and affidavits.” 80 Ill. Adm. Code
§1220.40(a)(1). Here, a review of the investigatory record reveals that the Board agent conducted
a thorough investigation in which the Charging Party provided documents in support of her unfair
labor practice charge and the Respondent submitted material in support of its position. Charging
Party’s appeal provides nothing more than conclusory remarks and statements that the
investigation was inadequate.
For the above reasons, we affirm the dismissal of the charge for the reasons stated by the
Executive Director subject to modification as discussed above.

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On April 3, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed the unfair labor practice
charge filed by Charging Party Mary White. Charging Party is employed by the Respondent Will
County Sheriff’s Department (“Employer”), as a Deputy Correctional Officer and is a member of
a bargaining unit represented by the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal
Employees, Council 31 (“AFSCME” or “Union”). Charging Party alleges that the Respondent
engaged in unfair labor practices within the meaning of Section 10(a) of the Illinois Public Labor
Relations Act (Act), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., when it discharged her in June 2022.
The Executive Director dismissed the charge as untimely filed and on the grounds that the
available evidence failed to raise issues of fact or law warranting a hearing. The Executive
Director found the charge untimely because it was filed outside the Act’s six-month limitation
period. She observed that Charging Party was discharged in June 2022, but did not file the instant
charge until February 2, 2025, nearly two years and eight months after the alleged unlawful
conduct. On the merits, the Executive Director construed the charge as one involving unlawful
discrimination and determined that there was insufficient evidence indicating that Charging Party
1

participated in protected activity or that the Employer took adverse action against her because of
such activity.
Charging Party timely filed an appeal of the dismissal. The Employer did not file a
response. On appeal, Charging Party seeks relief from the Executive Director’s timeliness
determination based on the health conditions that she was suffering from due to the COVID-19
virus. Charging Party also claims that she was discharged because she had filed a worker’s
compensation claim in April 2022, two months before her June 2022 discharge.
Upon review of the dismissal order, the appeal, and the record, we affirm the dismissal on
timeliness grounds for Charging Party’s appeal fails to undermine the Executive Director’s
findings that the charge was untimely filed. Essentially, Charging Party seeks tolling of the Act’s
six-month limitation period, ostensibly because she was unable to file the charge during that period
due to her illness from the COVID-19 virus. Section 11(a) of the Act provides that “no complaint
shall issue based upon any unfair labor practice occurring more than six-months prior to the filing
of a charge with the Board . . . .” 5 ILCS 315/11(a). Once the action has occurred, a charging
party is required to determine with due diligence if the Respondent’s action constitutes a violation
under the Act. Morales v. Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 241, 11 PERI ¶ 3010 (IL LLRB
1995). The limitation period can be tolled if there is evidence that the employer took steps to
prevent the employee from filing a charge, or if there was any event beyond the control of the
employee preventing the filing of a charge. See State of Ill., Dept. of Cent. Mgmt. Servs., (Eugene
Brown, Jr.), 19 PERI ¶ 105 (ILRB-SP 2003).
Here, Charging Party has provided scant evidence that she was precluded from filing her
charge within the Act’s limitation period because she was suffering from COVID-19 symptoms.
See id., 19 PERI ¶ 105 (ILRB-SP 2003) (rejecting a charging party’s contention that limitation
2

period should be tolled because he filed with the wrong agency). Accordingly, we find that the
Executive Director correctly dismissed the charge on timeliness grounds. Because we find the
charge to be untimely, we decline to reach the merits of the charge, as we lose jurisdiction over an
unfair labor practice charge filed outside the Act’s six-month limitations period. See id. (citing
Jones v. Ill. Educ. Labor Relations Bd., 272 Ill. App.3d 612, 621 (1st Dist. 1995) in which the
court noted that any decision on the merits by the Illinois Educational Labor Relations Board
would have been void for lack of jurisdiction).
For the above reasons, we affirm the dismissal on timeliness grounds.
BY THE STATE PANEL OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
STATE PANEL
On June 23, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed the unfair labor practice
charge filed by Charging Party Christopher Renteria on May 13, 2025. Charging Party is
employed by Respondent State of Illinois, Department of Central Management Services (Gaming
Board) (“Employer”) as a Gaming Special Agent (“GSA”) with the Illinois Gaming Board
(“Gaming Board”) and is a member of the bargaining unit represented by the American Federation
of State, County, and Municipal Employees (“Union”). Charging Party alleges that Respondent
engaged in unfair labor practices within the meaning of Section 10(a) of the Act when Respondent
failed to continue his “red-circled” pay after he was promoted to his target GSA title. “Red-
circled” pay refers to the Red-Circling Pay on Promotions provision (“Red Circling Provision”) of
the collective bargaining agreement between Respondent and Union (“CBA”) governing unit
member wages upon promotion.
Under the Red-Circling Provision of the CBA that was in effect before July 24, 2023, a
unit member taking a voluntary reduction to a trainee classification would receive either the in-
1

hire salary or his or her current salary. Once promoted to the desired target title, the unit member
would be placed at a salary step for the target title that would result in at least a $1 increase in pay.
Then on July 24, 2023, Respondent and the Union revised the Red-Circling Provision such that
the unit member would instead be placed at a step which represented a full step increase from his
previous position regardless of whether the new step placement resulted in a salary increase.
On January 19, 2024, Charging Party transferred to the position of Gaming Special Agent
Trainee with the Gaming Board from his position as a Corrections Treatment Officer Supervisor
(“CTOS”) with the Illinois Department of Corrections (“IDOC”). His salary was “red-circled,”
and he received $10,411 per month, the same salary he was earning as a CTOS at Step 8 of the
pay scale until he was promoted to the target title of GSA on April 22, 2025. Upon learning that
under the revised CBA provision, his pay would no longer be “red-circled” and that he would
instead receive $9,100 per month, the monthly pay rate for the highest step, Step 8, for the GSA
title, he filed a grievance. The Union withdrew the grievance at the third level, which precipitated
Charging Party’s filing of the charge in Case No. S-CB-25-039 which the Board voted to sustain
the Executive Director’s dismissal of the charge at its September 11, 2025 meeting.
The Executive Director dismissed the charge on timeliness grounds and on the grounds
that that the available evidence failed to raise issues of fact or law warranting a hearing. Regarding
timeliness, the Executive Director noted that Respondent notified Charging Party that he would no
longer receive his “red-circled” pay after his promotion to the GSA target title on October 10,
2024, more than 7 months before he filed the instant charge on May 14, 2025. On the merits, the
Executive Director construed the charge as one involving retaliation but found that the available
evidence failed to indicate that Respondent retaliated against Charging Party for participating in
protected, concerted activity. The Executive Director noted that, although filing a grievance can
2

constitute protected activity, Charging Party filed the grievance after the alleged retaliatory
conduct took place, and thus there was no evidence that Respondent took the alleged action against
Charging Party because he filed his grievance over his reduction in pay.
Charging Party timely filed an appeal of the dismissal. Respondent did not file a response.
Upon review of the dismissal order, the record, and Charging Party’s appeal, we find the
appeal without merit and sustain the dismissal for the reasons stated by the Executive Director as
further discussed below.
On appeal, Charging Party disputes both grounds for dismissal. First, Charging Party
contends that the Executive Director incorrectly determined that the six-month limitation period
began on October 10, 2024, the date a human resources representative informed him by telephone
that he would no longer be receiving his “red-circled” pay upon promotion to the GSA target title.
Charging Party asserts that the October 10, 2024, conversation was merely “informal and
informational,” and no effective date or exact amount of the new pay rate was discussed. Charging
Party contends that the Act’s limitation period is triggered when the conduct at issue “occurs or is
finalized,” which in this case was April 22, 2025, the effective date of his salary change, not by
his “informal” discussions on October 10, 2024 with his human resources representative. In
support, Charging Party cites to several Board and court cases, Service Employees Internation
Union, Local 46 (Evans), 16 PERI ¶ 3020 (IL LRB 2000), Jones v. Ill. Educ. Labor Relations Bd.,
et al., 272 Ill. App. 3d 612 (1st Dist. 1995), and Moore v. Ill. State Labor Relations Bd., et al., 206
Ill. App. 3d 327 (4th Dist. 1990).
Regarding the merits, Charging Party contends that the Executive Director erred in finding
that the evidence failed to indicate that Respondent engaged in any unlawful conduct. He points
to Section 310.220(f) of the Respondent’s Pay Plan which codified the language of the CBA’s Red
3

Circle Pay Provision in effect before July 24, 2023, claiming that Section 310.220(f) has the “force
and effect of law” and thus, the revised Red Circle Pay Provision, which contains conflicting
language from Section 310.220(f), is unenforceable. In support of this contention, Charging Party
cites to several court cases which he claims found agreements that are “contrary to law and public
policy” void and unenforceable. Charging Party further contends that Respondent’s application
of this “unenforceable” provision coerced him into accepting a pay cut, thereby interfering with
his rights in violation of Section 10(a)(1).
Finally, Charging Party contends that contrary to the Executive Director’s findings, he
engaged in concerted activity protected by the Act before he filed his grievance. He asserts that
he contacted a representative from his HR department in August 2024 about the Red Circle Pay
Provision and Section 310.22, who told him that “they have hardly ever dealt with this situation
and would need time to figure it out.” He further asserts that he “cited union-negotiated materials
to argue for my salary protections” and raised these concerns for other employees as well as for
himself. Moreover, Charging Party contends that has been harmed by the delay in disclosure of
the revised Red Circle Pay Provision, which was not publicly disclosed until the summer of 2024,
almost a year after the CBA between Respondent and the Union was ratified.
We find Charging Party’s contentions unavailing for they fail to undermine the Executive
Director’s determination that the allegations and available evidence failed to indicate that
Respondent engaged in conduct prohibited by the Act. We address the merits first because even
if we were to somehow find the charge timely filed, the alleged offending conduct does not
constitute an unfair labor practice.
Based on the charge itself, the available evidence and Charging Party’s contentions set
forth in his appeal, the alleged unfair labor practice appears to be Respondent’s application of the
4

July 24, 2023, revised Red Circling Pay Provision, which resulted in the reduction in Charging
Party’s wages, instead of the application of the “Red-circling” language set forth in Section
310.220(f) of the Employer’s administrative rules. Charging Party contends that such application
is an unfair labor practice because the July 24, 2023 agreement revising the Red Circling Pay
Provision conflicts with the Employer’s rules, thereby rendering that agreement void and
unenforceable. Charging Party also claims that such application constitutes unlawful coercion and
interference with his rights guaranteed by law. Essentially, Charging Party is asking this Board to
police the agreement executed by Respondent and the Union by fining the July 24, 2023 agreement
void and order Respondent to abide by the terms of the previous version of the agreement. We,
however, have long held that the Board does not police collective bargaining agreements, remedy
contractual breaches, or obtain specific enforcement of contract terms. Village of Creve Coeur, 3
PERI ¶ 2063 (IL SLRB 1987) (“We therefore do not believe that it is this Board’s functions[sic],
in an unfair labor practice context, to assume the role of policing collective bargaining agreements,
or to allow parties to use the Board’s processes to remedy alleged contractual breaches or to obtain
specific enforcement of contract terms.”).
Furthermore, as the Executive Director correctly concluded, the evidence failed to indicate
that Respondent’s application of the revised Red Circling Pay Provision which resulted in the
reduction in pay, was motivated by Charging Party’s participation in protected activity. Charging
Party’s grievance over his reduction in pay was filed. as the subject of the grievance indicates,
after Respondent applied the revised provision and reduced Charging Party’s pay. Moreover, the
activities Charging Party identifies in his appeal are not concerted as they primarily involved his
inquiries and discussions about how the revised “red-circling” provision would apply to him,
personally. There is no evidence, aside from his own assertions, that he took such actions on behalf
5

of other employees. Assuming for the sake of argument, that Charging Party did engage in
protected activity, there is no evidence that Respondent ceased to “red-circle” Charging Party’s
pay because Charging Party participated in such activities. Lastly, Charging Party’s remaining
arguments, inconsistent application of the revised agreement, coercion, are not supported by any
evidence sufficient to raise issues for hearing. According, the Executive Director correctly
dismissed the charge on the grounds the available evidence failed to raise issues warranting a
hearing.
For the above reasons, we affirm the Executive Director’s dismissal of the charge for the
reasons given therein.

DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On April 21, 2025, Executive Director Kimberly Stevens dismissed the unfair labor
practice charge filed by Charging Party Vicki Johnson who is employed by the Chicago Transit
Authority (“Employer” or “CTA”) as a full-time bus operator and is a member of the bargaining
unit represented by Respondent Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 241 (“Union”). The charge
alleges that the Respondent violated Section 10(b) of the Illinois Public Labor Relations Act
(“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., when it failed to keep her informed and involved at each step of the
governing collective bargaining agreement’s grievance/arbitration procedure related to the August
14, 2018 grievance that she filed challenging her discharge.
The Executive Director dismissed portions of the charge as untimely and dismissed the
remaining allegations on grounds that the available evidence failed to raise issues for hearing. She
first observed that the alleged conduct occurring before August 18, 2024, falls outside the six-
month limitation period set forth in Section 11(a), and thus, is not actionable. The Executive
Director further observed that the available evidence indicated that the Union conducted grievance
1

meetings on August 23, 2018, and September 4, 2019, and that the Union informed Charging Party
on March 10, 2020, that it had conducted a pre-arbitration meeting. Based on this evidence, the
Executive Director reasoned that Charging Party had knowledge of the grievance meetings
conducted in her absence on March 12, 2020, nearly 5 years before the Charging Party filed her
charge on February 18, 2025, and dismissed the allegations related to the Union’s failure to allow
the Charging Party to attend grievance meetings.
The Executive Director dismissed the remaining allegations because she determined that
the Charging Party failed to provide evidence indicating that the Respondent violated the Act. She
observed that the allegations that the Respondent violated the Union’s bylaws by excluding her
from the grievance meeting involves internal union matters over which the Board has no
jurisdiction. Fraternal Order of Police, Lodge #7, 22 PERI ¶ 63 (IL LRB-LP 2006). Noting the
intentional misconduct standard in duty of fair representation cases and a union’s discretion in
grievance handling under Section 6(d) of the Act, the Executive Director also found that the
Charging Party failed to present evidence that the Respondent took any adverse representation
against her as the Respondent advanced the grievance to the arbitration step of the grievance
process, which is currently pending. Moreover, the Executive Director observed that Respondent’s
alleged failure to communicate with Charging Party and to update her on the status of her grievance
is insufficient to establish a causal connection, citing Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 241
(Spratt), 31 PERI ¶ 121 (IL LRB-LP 2015).
The Charging Party timely appealed. The Respondent did not file a response.
On appeal, the Charging Party maintains that Respondent has treated her unfairly and fails
to adequately communicate with her about her grievance. The Charging Party acknowledges that
the Union advised her that her grievance was denied after going through expedited arbitration and
2

then later informed her that the grievance was sent to expedited arbitration in error. She further
asserts that she contacted the Union’s international office and was told that the international was
without authority to intervene in the process.
Upon review of the record, the dismissal order, and Charging Party’s appeal, we affirm the
dismissal of the charge for the reasons given by the Executive Director. The appeal lacks merit
for it fails to provide any evidence or cogent argument that undermines the Executive Director’s
determinations.
On the timeliness issue, although the Charging Party claims she has sent letters annually to
the Union asking for the status of her grievance starting in April 2020, the appeal does not
specifically address the Executive Director’s dismissal of the allegations pertaining to the
Respondent’s failure to allow the Charging Party to attend the grievance meetings as time barred.
Section 11(a) of the Act provides that “no complaint shall issue based upon any unfair labor
practice occurring more than six-months prior to the filing of a charge with the Board . . . .” 5
ILCS 315/11(a). Once the action has occurred, the Charging Party is required to determine with
due diligence if the Respondent’s action constitute a violation under the Act. Morales v.
Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 2, 11 PERI ¶ 3010 (IL LLRB 1995). The limitation period
can be tolled if there is evidence that the union took steps to prevent the employee from filing a
charge, or if there was any event beyond the control of the employee preventing the filing of a
charge. State of Ill., Dept. of Central Mgmt. Servs., (Eugene Brown, Jr.), 19 PERI ¶ 105 (ILRB-
SP 2003). Nothing in the Charging Party’s appeal serves as evidence or argument that the Union
prevented the Charging Party from filing a charge or that she was precluded from filing a charge
within the six-month limitation period. Accordingly, the Executive Director correctly dismissed
these allegations as untimely.
3

Regarding the remaining allegations, although the Charging Party identifies in her appeal
several instances that she contends demonstrates the Union’s failure to communicate, none of these
instances serves to undermine any of the Executive Director’s findings, analysis, or conclusions
that the Union’s conduct violated Section 10(b) of the Act. As the Executive Director correctly
noted, the Charging Party appears to be upset at the lengthy grievance arbitration process resulting
from the erroneous expedited arbitration. Moreover, the investigation revealed that the Union
corrected the error, and that the arbitration of the Charging Party’s grievance is currently pending.
Accordingly, we find that the Executive Director correctly dismissed the charge.
For the reasons set forth above, we affirm the dismissal of the charges for the reasons stated
by the Executive Director.
